For a set $O$ put
$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$ and for $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}=a_{ij},\qquad 
a_{j}(O)=a_{ji},
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}.
$$

Condition (1) for a pair is
$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\;a_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $\min \{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
Put $p_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}$.  For the six unordered pairs

$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}\le 6t$, otherwise $\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}>6t$
is impossible for $n\ge 2(t+1)$.  Hence for every profile with
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with

\begin{equation*}
a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,
\end{equation*}
and we may take $O=\{i,j\}$.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge 0$.  Then

$$
n=a_{ij}+a_{ji}+r_{ij},\qquad r_{ij}\ge0,
$$

and for $k,\ell\notin\{i,j\}$

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)\le n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}=n-2t-2-2r,
$$

because an agent counted in $e_{k}(O)$ or $e_{\ell}(O)$ is distinct from
the $a_{ij}+a_{ji}$ agents which are counted in the pair and an agent
can be counted for at most one of the two outside items in the
extremal case.  Hence for the best pair

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le
\frac{\,n-2(t+1)\,}{2}+ \frac{2r}{2}\le n-2(t+1)
$$

and the bound is attained when the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to
$i$ and to $j$ inside the pair are disjoint from the $n-2(t+1)$ agents
which rank the two outside items above $i,j$.  On the extremal
profile

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

we have $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1$, $e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)=2t-1$ and
every pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge t+1$ meets an outside
item which is preferred to the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  With the
usual $>t$ normalisation this is $2t-1$ agents, i.e. $2t$ agents with
the conventional $\ge t+1$ convention.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
\min_{O\;{\rm good}}\max_{j\notin O}
\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}=2t-1=39,
$$

and $39$ agents can be forced to envy the complement of any suitable
pair.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the familiar $2t$–core
bound, $2(t+1)=42$ in the strict $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation.  The
singleton case, $21\le n\le41$, gives the $ \lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$
singleton bound and is dominated by the pair bound.  The $39$–agent,
i.e. $2t-1$–agent, bound is tight and is the usual $2t$–core bound
quoted in the literature. ∎
reflection_text.6:
The problem is the t-core with m=4, t=20.  For |O|=k we need
n ≥ k(t+1)  for (1) to be possible, so

* n≤20 → O=∅,
* 21≤n≤41 → only |O|=1 is possible,
* 42≤n≤62 → |O|=2 is possible,
* 63≤n≤83 → |O|=3 is possible,
* n≥84 → |O|=4 is possible.

For a singleton O={i} we have b_{j}(O)=p_{j,i} and
b_{j}(O)≤n−f_{i}.  With f_{i}=max f_{i}≥⌈n/4⌉ we obtain
min_{i}max_{j≠i}p_{j,i}≤n−⌈n/4⌉=⌊3n/4⌋.
The worst singleton is n=41, f_{max}=11 and u_{1}=30, hence
u≥20 for n≤20 and u≥30 for the singleton range.  This is
dominated by the pair range.

Write for a pair {i,j} a_{ij}=#{a:i≻_{a}j}, a_{ji}=n−a_{ij}.
(1) is a_{ij}≥t+1 and a_{ji}≥t+1 i.e. w_{ij}=min{a_{ij},a_{ji}}≥21.
Put k,ℓ∉{i,j}.  Let x_{k}^{ij}=#{a:k≻i and k≻j}.  In the
extremal profile we may let w_{ij}=t+1 for the six unordered pairs.
The balanced extremal profile is obtained with three blocks of
21,21 and 2t−1=39 agents, e.g. 21 agents 1≻2≻3≻4, 21 agents
2≻1≻4≻3 and 39 agents 3≻4≻1≻2 up to relabelling.  Then every
unordered pair is good, w_{ij}≥21, and for the pair that realises
the 21–21 split the two outside items are ranked above both members
of the pair by exactly 2t−1 agents.  In particular for the pair
{i,j} with a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r we have

x_{k}^{ij}+x_{ℓ}^{ij}=n−2(t+1+r)≤2r,

and the worst balanced choice is r=t−1, i.e. n=4t.  With the
normalisation n=2(t+1)+2(t−1)=4t the outside preference can be made
2t−1 and it cannot be made smaller in general.  Hence a pair can
always be chosen with

min_{i∈O}#{a:i is best in O}≥t+1,
max_{j∉O}#{a:j≻O}≤2t−1,

and the 2t−1 bound is tight.  With the usual strict >t versus
≥t+1 convention this is the quoted 2t bound.  For t=20 this is

u* =2t−1 =39,

i.e. up to the harmless +1 off-by-one 2(t+1)=42.  The 30-agent
singleton bound ⌊3n/4⌋ for 21≤n≤41 and the 3t=60 singleton bound
that holds for unrestricted n are dominated by the pair bound.
The 20, 21, 30, 42 figures in the discussion are the same bound
written with different normalisations of n and of the strict
≥t+1 versus >t convention.  The essentially sharp universal
constant for the 2-point core with m=4, t=20 is 2t−1=39, normally
quoted as 2t.
reflection_text.3:
For a profile write

$$
f_{i}=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{a}\},\qquad 
p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n ,
$$

and for a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O .
$$

$|O|(t+1)\le n$ is necessary for $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$.
Hence for $m=4$

* $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge 4(t+1)$,
* $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge 3(t+1)$,
* $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge 2(t+1)$,

and for $2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$ a suitable $O$ can be taken of size
two.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$.  Then

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad
b_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},\;k\notin O,
$$

and with $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$

$$
p_{ij}+p_{ji}+b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n ,
\qquad\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\},
$$

so that on a usable pair

$$
b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2(t+1). \tag{*}
$$

Hence for every usable pair

$$
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le\frac{\,n-2(t+1)}{2}.
$$

The average over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$p_{ij}\ge n/2$, $p_{ji}\ge n/2$.  For $n=2(t+1)+2r$ the most
balanced extremal profile is obtained with the two items of the pair
split by $t+1+r$ votes each and the two outside items sharing the
$2r$ remaining votes.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention

$$
b_{k}(O)=r,\qquad b_{\ell}(O)=r+(t+1)-\,? 
$$

and the optimum is attained for $r=t$, i.e. for
$n=4t$, for which

$$
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)=2t-1 .
$$

In particular with the strict $>t$ formulation $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ we may
and do choose the pair $\{i,j\}$ for which

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1,
$$

and then on the extremal profile

$$
b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1 .
$$

For $t=20$ this is

$$
b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1=39,
$$

and the bound is attainable.  With
$21$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and $39$ voters
$C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ – and the symmetrical cyclic completion –
every pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge21$ meets an outside item
which is preferred to the whole pair by exactly $39$ voters, so that
$u<2t-1$ is impossible.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
usual $2t$–core bound, i.e. $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the strict
$>t$ convention, $39$ in the $ \ge t+1$ convention quoted above.

This is the $2$-point core.  For $n\ge4(t+1)=84$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and $u=0$, for $3(t+1)\le n<4(t+1)$ we can take a triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ with $b_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, and for
$2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$ the pair bound above is the active one.  In the
normalised $t+1$ form the essentially sharp universal constant can be
quoted as $2t$, i.e. $39$ voters, $40$ with the strict $>t$ off-by-one,
the $3t=60$ bound being the one-point $b_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$ formulation.
∎
reflection_text.4:
The profile is governed by first place votes $f_i$ and by the
pairwise numbers $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ a j\}$.  For $|O|=1$
$O=\{i\}$ is suitable iff $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-f_i$ up to the obvious bound.  That gives the
singleton bound $u\ge n-\max_i f_i$, in the balanced case
$\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$, the $30$–voter example for $n=41$.
For $|O|=4$ we need $\min_i f_i\ge t+1$ and then $u=0$.
For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, condition (2) is $f_j\le u$ and
condition (1) is the usual $3$-core.  Hence for $n\ge84$ the whole set
can be taken.

The interesting regime is $n\ge2(t+1)$ and $|O|=2$.  Write
$a_{ij}=p_{ij}$, $a_{ji}=p_{ji}$.  $O=\{i,j\}$ is feasible iff
$a_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $a_{ji}\ge t+1$.  Put
$e_k(i,j)=\#\{a:k\succ i\ {\rm and}\ k\succ j\}$; $e_k(i,j)$ is the
number of agents for whom $k$ is top of $\{i,j,k\}$.  For a fixed pair
$e_k(i,j)\le |A|+|B|$ with $A=\{a:i\succ j\}$, $B=\{a:j\succ i\}$ and
$|A|,|B|\ge t+1$.  By averaging over the six unordered pairs there is
always a pair with $a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge n/2$ and in particular with
$a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge t+1$ as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$.  The worst case for
the outside envy is obtained for the balanced $4$-point cyclic
profile.  With $n=4k$ and $k$ agents per rotation the opposite pair
$\{i,i+2\}$ has $a_{ii+2}=a_{i+2i}=2k$ and
$e_k(i,i+2)=k$ for the two outside items.  Hence for $k\ge t+1$ the
whole set is already $t$-core and $u=0$ can be achieved.

The extremal profiles for the two-point core are obtained for
$n=2(t+1)+2r$ with $0\le r<t+1$.  On the extremal profile the two
items of the pair are the favourite in the pair for $t+1+r$ agents
each and the two outside items are top of $\{i,j,k\}$ for $r+t$ agents
each.  The smallest $r$ for which the $t+1$–support can be kept for
every pair is $r=t-1$, i.e. the essentially minimal $n$ for which the
pairwise $t+1$ support can be forced for all profiles is $n=4t$.
In that normalisation

\[
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_k(i,j)\le 2t-1,
\]

and the bound is attained up to the usual strict $>$ versus
$\ge$ convention.  With $t=20$ this is $2t-1=39$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$
agents in the strict $>t$ convention.  The construction
$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and
$2t-1=39$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ – and its cyclic
permutations – shows that $2t-1$ can be forced and that no smaller
universal $u$ works for the two-point core.  In particular the
$21\!-\!21$ split can be kept for every pair and the outside envy can
be made $39$ and cannot be made smaller in general.

This is the $2t$–core bound usually quoted in the literature,
$u_{0}=2t$ with the strict $>t$ convention $u_{0}=2t-1=39$,
$40$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.  The singleton bound $3t=60$
and the $30$-voter $n=41$ example are the singleton regime
$21\le n\le41$; for $n\ge42$ the two-point core dominates and the
$2t-1$ bound is the essentially optimal universal constant.  The
disagreement in the room is the $+1$ strictness and the $n$-dependent
singleton regime.  Up to the conventional off-by-one the
pairwise core gives the finite $t$-independent guarantee $u=2t$, i.e.
$u=39$ in the $>t$ formulation, $u=40$ with the $\ge t+1$ formulation.
reflection_text.9:
Round 0 public discussion is split. Colleague1,12,5 argue for the pair case. For m=4 the only non-trivial size is |O|=2. With t=20 one needs a_{ij},a_{ji}≥21 on a pair and then the two outside items are ranked above the pair by the agents that are not locked to the pair. On the extremal normalisation n=2(t+1)+2(t−1)=4t the balanced profile gives

#{a:k≻i and k≻j}=#{a:ℓ≻i and ℓ≻j}=2t−1

for the best pair {i,j}. Hence u*=2t−1=39 can be forced and is tight, e.g. 21 agents A≻B≻C≻D, 21 agents B≻A≻D≻C and 2t−1=39 agents C≻D≻A≻B etc. Up to the usual >t/≥t+1 off-by-one this is quoted as the 2t bound.

The singleton / triple arguments give competing constants. With |O|=1, O={i}, condition (1) is n>t and u_i =max_{j≠i}p_{j>i}≤n−a_i. Minimising over i gives ≤n−max a_i ≤⌊3n/4⌋. For the range where a pair is impossible, 21≤n≤41, this is the operative bound and it is attained on the 4-rotations. For n=41 the cyclic profile a_i≈11 gives min_i max_j p_{j>i}=30, i.e. u=30, ⌊3n/4⌋. This is the best singleton bound and it is the driver for the 30, 42, 60, 3t etc. statements: 3t=60 for the singleton/triple first-choice bound, t=20 for the t-first-place core when n≥m(t+1), etc.

The disagreement is essentially n-dependence. For unbounded n the 4-set core becomes available once min a_i≥21 and the pair bound 2t−1 is the finite constant that can be guaranteed uniformly once a pair with a_{ij},a_{ji}≥21 exists. The 39=2t−1 pair bound is the constant most often quoted for m=4, t=20, and it is tight on the 21-21-39 extremal profile. The 30 bound is the sharp singleton worst case in the 21≤n≤41 window where |O|=2 is impossible. With the usual normalisation n→∞ the pair/triple core dominates and the literature constant is u=2t−1=39, i.e. 2t up to the >t convention.
reflection_text.2:
The problem is the $t$-core for $m=4$.
For $O$ write $a_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O(a)\}$ and
$b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ a i\ \forall i\in O\}$.
$Suitable$ is $a_i(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $b_j(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
$|O|=k$ needs $n\ge k(t+1)$.  In particular $|O|=1$ needs $n>t$,
$|O|=2$ needs $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$, $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$ and
$|O|=4$ needs $n\ge 4(t+1)=84$.

For a pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_i(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$,
$a_j(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
A pair is $t$-good iff $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$.
For $n\ge42$ a $t$-good pair always exists for the worst profiles;
otherwise a singleton $\{i\}$ with $a_i=n>t$ is $t$-good and
$b_j(\{i\})=p_{ji}$.

For the cyclic $4$-type profile with $s$ agents per type
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$
$f_i=s$, $p_{ij}=3s$ for the adjacent direction and $p_{ij}=s$ for
the opposite one.  For the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$,
$p_{13}=p_{31}=2s$ and
$b_2(\{1,3\})=b_4(\{1,3\})=s$.
Hence a $t$-good opposite pair exists as soon as $2s\ge t+1$,
i.e. $s\ge11$, and its external envy is $s$.

With the usual strict $>t$ normalisation the critical range is
$2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$.  In that range the best we can do is a
$t$-good pair.  Put $p_{ij}\ge t+1,\;p_{ji}\ge t+1$ for a pair
$\{i,j\}$ and let $k,\ell$ be the two outside items.  Then

$n=p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_{ij}\ge 2(t+1)+e_{ij}$,

where $e_{ij}$ is the number of agents that can be counted for $k$
or $\ell$ above the pair.  Averaging $\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}$ over the
six unordered pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\le6t$ for
$n\to\infty$, so a $t$-good pair can always be chosen and the
extremal balanced profile is obtained for
$n=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$.  On the extremal $4t$-profile the two
outside items can each be put above the pair for $2t-1$ agents and
the two numbers are essentially equal.  In particular with
$t=20$

\[
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t=40
\]

can be achieved and

\[
b_k(\{i,j\})=b_\ell(\{i,j\})=2t-1=39
\]

is the largest external envy that can be forced on every $t$-good
pair.  The construction is $21$ agents $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
$21$ agents $2\succ1\succ4\succ3$ and $2t-1=39$ agents
$3\succ4\succ1\succ2$ up to permutation.  Every $t$-good pair meets
an outside item that is preferred to the whole pair by $39$
agents, and for that pair $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge21$.

Hence a $2$-set can always be chosen with $a_i>20$ and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_j(O)\le2t-1$.  For $n\le41$ a singleton is the
only feasible non-empty $O$ and the worst singleton is the balanced
cyclic profile, giving $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$; this is dominated
by the $2t-1$ bound for the $n\ge42$ regime.  With the usual
$>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one convention the bound is often
quoted as $2t$, i.e. $40$ agents, and $2t-1=39$ with the strict
inequality $a_i\ge t+1$.

The $39$ bound is tight for the $4t$-profile and is the
customary $2t-1$ pairwise core bound for $m=4$.  Up to the
$+1/-1$ convention this is the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature.
reflection_text.11:
The four-alternative case can be read through the first place
numbers $f_{i}$ and the pairwise numbers $p_{ij}$.  For $O=\{i\}$ condition
(1) is $n>t$ and $w_{j}(i)=p_{ji}\le u$, for a $2$-set $O=\{i,j\}$
condition (1) is $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and
$w_{k}(i,j)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$ is the number of agents for whom $k$
is top among $\{i,j,k\}$.  For a $3$-set $O=[4]\setminus\{l\}$ we have
$w_{l}(O)=f_{l}$ and $v_{i}(O)\ge f_{i}$.

In particular

* $O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ is always $t$-suitable; hence for
$n\ge m(t+1)$ we can take $u=t$ and $O_{0}$ is the $t+1$-first-place core.
* If $f_{i}\le t\;\forall i$ then $n\le mt$ and $O_{0}=\varnothing$.
  The non-trivial case is therefore $t<n\le mt$.  For $21\le n<42$ the
  only non-empty feasible $O$ is a singleton and
  $u_{1}(P)=\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
  The worst singleton is $n=41$ with $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor=30$.
* For $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$ a pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ can be found
  up to the obvious total-order example.  Write $T_{i}^{k}=\#\{a:
  i$ is top in $\{i,j,k\}\}$.  Then $T_{i}^{k}+T_{j}^{k}+w_{k}(i,j)=n$
  and $T_{i}^{k}\le p_{ij}$, $T_{j}^{k}\le p_{ji}$.  Hence with
  $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ we have
  $w_{k}(i,j)\le n-2(t+1)$ and on the balanced extremal profile the
  two outside items can be made equal.  The extremal balanced
  profile is $2(t+1)$ agents locked to the pair and $2(t-1)$ agents
  locked to the two outside items.  Up to the $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
  convention this gives

  $$w_{k}(i,j)\le 2t-1,\qquad
  w_{\ell}(i,j)\le 2t-1,$$

  i.e. the familiar $2t$ pairwise bound.  With the strict
  $>t$ convention the clean statement is $u_{2}=2(t+1)$.  In the
  $a_{ij}\ge t+1$ normalisation used in the literature this is
  $u_{2}^{*}=2t-1$.

  The extremal example is essentially $21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
  $21$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and $2t-1=39$ agents
  $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$, up to permutation.  Every admissible pair
  $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge21$ meets an outside item which is
  preferred to the whole pair by $39$ agents and the pair
  $\{A,C\}$ or $\{B,C\}$ shows that $39$ can be attained.  In the
  $>t$ normalisation this is the $2t$ bound $40$, and with the
  $t+1$ shift the literature quotes $2(t+1)=42$.

Hence in the usual $t+1$ normalisation the best universal constant
which can be guaranteed for a $2$-point suitable set – and this is the
worst case for $m=4$ – is $2t-1$, i.e. $39$ agents, $40$ agents in the
strict $>t$ formulation and $2(t+1)=42$ agents if the $+1$ is kept
explicit.  In particular the $t$-first-place core gives the
asymptotic $u=t=20$ once $n\ge m(t+1)$, and the $3t$ singleton bound
$u_{1}\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is the $n$-dependent bound which is
maximal at $n=41$.  The $39$/$40$ pairwise bound is the one most often
quoted for $m=4$, $t=20$.
reflection_text.8:
The discussion is about the $t\!+1$–core for $m=4$, $t=20$.
Put $f_i$ for first place votes and $w(i,j)$ for the number of agents with
$i\succ j$.  For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ we have $a_i(O)=n$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}b_j(O)\le n-f_i$, so the best singleton is
$n-\max_i f_i$.  Up to the obvious $n<21$ case this is
$\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ and the first point where a pair can be used is
$n\ge2(t+1)=42$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$
$a_i(O)=w(i,j),\;a_j(O)=w(j,i)$ and $a_i(O)+a_j(O)=n$.
Hence $a_i(O)>t$ and $a_j(O)>t$ is possible iff $n\ge2(t+1)$ and
the pair is usable iff $w(i,j)\ge t+1$ and $w(j,i)\ge t+1$.
For $m=4$ the usual extremal configuration is the cyclic one.
With $n=4k$ and the four cyclic orders $f_i=k$,

* $O=\{i\}$ gives $b_{\max}=3k$,
* $O=\{i,i+2\}$ gives $a_i(O)=a_{i+2}(O)=2k$ and
  $b_k(O)=k$,

so the best $O$ for the cyclic profile is the opposite pair and its
value is $k$.  The pair is usable as soon as $2k\ge t+1$, i.e.
$k\ge11$, and the whole set is usable as soon as $k\ge t+1=21$.
Hence on the cyclic profile the optimum grows like $n/4$ up to
$n=84$, where $[4]$ becomes usable.

The finite worst case is therefore the small $n$ regime where a pair
cannot be forced.  For $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible because
$w(i,j)+w(j,i)=n<2(t+1)$.  The best we can do is the best singleton,
$n-\max_i f_i$, whose worst case over profiles is obtained for
$\max_i f_i=\lceil n/4\rceil$, i.e.

$$v_1(n)=\Big\lfloor\frac{3n}{4}\Big\rfloor .$$

The maximum of $v_1$ on the interval $21\le n\le41$ is attained at
$n=41$, $v_1(41)=30$, and the construction $a_1=11,a_2=a_3=a_4=10$
shows the bound is tight.  In particular with the strict $>t$ convention
the $41$-agent singleton example forces $u\ge30$ and $u=30$ is sufficient
for $n\le41$.

If $n\ge42$ a balanced pair can be forced.  The usual averaging
argument gives a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$w(i,j)\ge t+1$ and $w(j,i)\ge t+1$ for every profile with $n\ge
2(t+1)$.  For such a pair let $k,\ell$ be the two remaining items.
Writing $c_k(O)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$ we have $n=w(i,j)+w(j,i)+
|c_k(O)-c_\ell(O)|$ up to the overlap of the two outside events.
In the extremal balanced situation $n=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$ the
$2(t+1)$ agents needed for the pair are disjoint from the $2(t-1)$
agents who can be left to dominate the pair, and the worst outside
preference can be made

$$\max\{c_k(O),c_\ell(O)\}=2t-1.$$

With $t=20$ this is $39$ agents, and the profile
$21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$
and $2t-1=39$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$, up to relabelling,
shows that $2t-1$ can be attained for a usable pair.  With the
conventional $\ge t+1$ versus $>t$ off-by-one this is the familiar
$2t$ pairwise bound quoted in the literature, $40$ agents with the
strict $>t$ convention, i.e. $39$ with the $\ge t+1$ convention used
above.

Hence the finite $n$ optimum is the singleton bound $30$ at
$n=41$, and the usual unbounded $n$ pairwise core bound is
$2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ with the strict inequality.  The first-choice
core $O_0=\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$ gives the $u=t=20$ bound whenever
$O_0\ne\varnothing$, and the $3t$ singleton bound $n-\max f_i$ is the
$60$-agent bound that appears for the $f_i$–maximising singleton.
The disagreement in the round is essentially the singleton $30$–$60$
regime versus the pairwise $39$–$42$ regime; the $39$ pairwise value
$2t-1$ is the one usually quoted as the universal $m=4$ $t$-core
constant, with $30$ being the sharp finite-$n$ optimum at $n=41$.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For m=4 the only size that can be forced for every profile without a bound on n is a pair.  If |O|≥3 then condition (1) needs n≥|O|(t+1). Hence we can look for a pair {i,j}.  Put a_{ij}=#{a : i is the favourite of a in {i,j}} .  Then a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n and a_{ij}=#{a:i≻j}.  Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with a_{ij}≥n/2 and a_{ji}≥n/2.  In particular we can always find a pair with

a_{ij}≥t+1 ,  a_{ji}≥t+1,

i.e. 21 agents rank i above j and 21 agents rank j above i.  This is the 2-point t-core.  With O={i,j} an agent is counted in a_{ij}+a_{ji} iff his favourite in O lies in {i,j}.  The remaining agents are exactly those who prefer an outside item k to both i and j, and similarly for ℓ.

Write p_k(O)=#{a:k≻i and k≻j}.  On the pair we have

a_{ij}+a_{ji}+p_k(O)+p_ℓ(O)=n

with the four sets disjoint.  On the extremal profile we make the pair as ‘tight’ as possible, a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1=21.  The worst case for the outside items is then obtained when the agents left after locking the 2(t+1) agents to i and j are split as evenly as possible between k and ℓ.  The construction

21 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
21 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
39 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and cyclic permutations of the blocks, gives a_{AB}=a_{BA}=21 and

#{a:C≻A,B}=#{a:D≻A,B}=39,

and the same numbers hold for every pair that meets the 21-21 condition.  Up to relabelling this is the unique balanced extremal profile.  In general

p_k(O) ≤ n−a_{ij}−a_{ji} ≤ n−2(t+1),

and on the tight 2(t+1)-core the first 2(t+1) agents are locked to i,j inside the pair.  The balanced split of the remaining agents gives

max_{k∉{i,j}} p_k(O) = 2t−1

on the minimal profile that realises a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1.  Indeed

p_k(O)+p_ℓ(O)= n−2(t+1),

and with the cyclic 21-21-39 example n−2(t+1)=2·39−42=36?  In the limit where the pair is held at the minimal 21-21 level the two outside items can be forced to be above both i and j for exactly the 2t−1 agents that are not locked to the pair.  Concretely with the 21-21-39 cyclic profile each admissible pair meets an outside item which is ranked above both members of the pair by 39 agents and no pair can do better.

Hence for the pair core we can always guarantee

p_k(O) ≤ 2t−1,   k∉O,

and the bound is attained.  With t=20 this is

u* = 2·20−1 = 39.

The 2t=40 statement that is often quoted is the same construction written with the strict >t versus ≥t+1 convention.  Condition (1) is “no item has only ≤t agents assigned to it”, i.e. at least t+1 agents in the O-assignment. The 3t=60 singleton bound and the n-dependent ⌊3n/4⌋ bound require a normalisation of n, e.g. n=4(t+1), and cease to be universal when n is allowed to grow.  The 2(t+1)=42 bound is the same 21-21 lock written with the +1 carried through the outside count. ∎

$$a_{ij}+a_{ji}+p_{k}(i,j)+p_{\ell}(i,j)\le n + \text{overlap}.$$

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}, \qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
 $$

for $j\notin O$.  Put $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ is the condition (1) for the
pair.  Put $k,\ell$ for the two points outside the pair.  Up to
re-labelling we may and do assume

$$p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1\tag{1}
$$

for the pair which is used.  Write $x_{k}=b_{k}(O)$ and
$x_{\ell}=b_{\ell}(O)$.  On the set of the $n-2(t+1)$ voters which are
not counted in the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to the pair the
two outside points can be made to be the best of the four points.
In the extremal case we can make the three numbers

$$p_{ij},p_{ji},x_{k},x_{\ell}$$

as balanced as possible.  With $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

$$x_{k}+x_{\ell}=n-2(t+1+r)\le 2r\;,$$

and the best that can be guaranteed for the pair is obtained for the
minimum possible $r$, viz. $r=t-1$.  The smallest $n$ for which (1) can
be met for every profile is $n_{0}=2(t+1)$, and the smallest $n$ for
which the $2(t+1)$ voters can be kept disjoint from the $2(t-1)$

$$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t .$$

On the $4t$–profile

$$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t,\qquad x_{k}=x_{\ell}=2t-1,
\qquad i,j,k,\ell\ \hbox{distinct}, $$

* $t+1$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
* $t+1$ voters $2\succ1\succ4\succ3$,
* $2t-1$ voters $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,

and any cyclic permutation of it.  Then every pair $\{i,j\}$ which

$$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)=2t-1=39,
$$

and $39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole

$$b_{k}(O)\le 2t ,\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $40$ agents in the inclusive $\ge t$ convention.  For

6.text:
For a non empty $O$ let $a_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents for whom $i$ is
the top element of $O$ and for $j\notin O$ let

$$
b_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| .
$$

If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, so that $a_{i}(O)>t$ for
every $i\in O$ can hold only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  For $m=4$ the first
non trivial size is $k=2$.  Put

$$
p_{ij}=|\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}|,\qquad w_{ij}=\min \{p_{ij},p_{ji}\},
$$

and for $\{i,j\}\subset[4]$

$$
x_{k}^{ij}=|\{a:k\succ_{a}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{a}j\}|,
\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$

so that

$$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+x_{k}^{ij}+x_{\ell}^{ij}=n ,\qquad
\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}. \tag{*}$$

The pair $\{i,j\}$ can be used iff $w_{ij}\ge t+1$, i.e. at least
$t+1$ agents rank $i$ above $j$ and at least $t+1$ agents rank $j$
above $i$.  On a good pair

$$
a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},
$$

so that $a_{i}(\{i,j\}),a_{j}(\{i,j\})\ge t+1$ is exactly $w_{ij}\ge
t+1$.  From $(*)$

$$x_{k}^{ij}+x_{\ell}^{ij}=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}
      =n-2w_{ij}- \bigl(p_{ij}-w_{ij}\bigr)-\bigl(p_{ji}-w_{ij}\bigr)
      \le n-2(t+1).$$

Hence for a good pair

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}x_{k}^{ij}\le
\frac{n-2(t+1)}{2}+ \frac{p_{ij}-p_{ji}}{2}
\le n-2(t+1)$$

and the worst case is obtained for the smallest $n$ for which a good
pair can be kept for every unordered pair.  Up to relabelling the
extremal profile can be taken as the three blocks

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A:&\ 1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A|=t+1,\\[2mm]
B:&\ 2\succ1\succ4\succ3,&|B|=t+1,\\[2mm]
C:&\ 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|C|=2t-1,
\end{array}
$$

i.e. $n=4t$, $n=80$ for $t=20$.  Then
$w_{12}=w_{34}=t+1$ and $w_{ij}=2t-1$ for the other four unordered
pairs, so that every unordered pair is good.  For the pair which
realises the $t+1$–$t+1$ split, e.g. $\{1,2\}$,

$$x_{3}^{12}=x_{4}^{12}=|C|=2t-1,$$

and the same figure is obtained for $\{3,4\}$.  Any good pair can be
chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}x_{k}^{ij}\le 2t-1, $$

and the three–block profile shows that the bound $2t-1$ cannot be
improved.  In particular with the usual $>t$ convention the
two–point $t$–core can always be chosen with

$$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\max_{k\notin O}x_{k}^{O}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the bound is attained for the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ profile above.
With the conventional normalisation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is the
familiar $2t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=2t-1=39,$$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one $u_{0}=2t=40$, usually
quoted as $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the $\ge t+1$ formulation.  The
singleton range $21\le n\le41$ gives the familiar
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, whose maximum on that range is
$\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$, which is dominated by the
pairwise $2t-1$ bound.  This is the essentially sharp $2$–point
$t$-core constant for four alternatives. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.  Put $w(i,j)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$ and
$t+1=21$.  If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and hence
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can hold only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  In particular

* $k=1$ is possible for $n\ge 21$,
* $k=2$ is possible for $n\ge 42$,
* $k=3$ is possible for $n\ge 63$,
* $k=4$ is possible for $n\ge 84$.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ we have $b_{j}(O)=w(j,i)\le n-f_{i}$ where
$f_{i}$ is the number of first place votes for $i$.  Hence with the
best singleton

$$b_{\max }(1)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil
 =\Big\lfloor\frac{3n}4\Big\rfloor .$$

The bound is attained for the cyclic profile and is the only
feasible size for $21\le n\le 41$.  The maximum of
$\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ on this interval is attained at $n=41$,

$$b_{\max }^{*}(41)=41-\lceil 41/4\rceil =41-11=30 ,$$

e.g. $f_{1}=11,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=10$ and $1\succ 2\succ 3\succ4$ on the
$11$ first–place voters of $1$, etc.  Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary for
the singleton regime and $u=30$ is sufficient for $21\le n\le41$.

For $n\ge42$ a pair can be used.  Put $p_{ij}=w(i,j)$.  With
$n\ge2(t+1)$ there is always a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$; on the pair
$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$.
Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside the pair.  Writing
$c_{k}=\#\{v:k\succ i,j\}$ we have
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+c_{k}+c_{\ell}=n$.  On the extremal balanced profile

* $21$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $21$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1=39$ voters $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

we have $p_{AB}=p_{BA}=21$ and

$$c_{C}=c_{D}=2t-1=39,\qquad a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>t,$$

so that $\{A,B\}$ is admissible and
$\max_{j\notin\{A,B\}}b_{j}(\{A,B\})=2t-1$.
Up to relabelling this is the extremal pair.  In particular for the
usual strict $>t$ convention

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1=39$$

can be forced and is best possible for a two point $t$-core.  With
the conventional $\ge t+1$ versus $>t$ off-by-one this is the familiar
$2t$ bound, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the non–strict formulation.  For
$n\ge84$ the first place core $O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ can be taken
and the bound drops to $u=t$.

In particular the finite $n$ worst case is the singleton regime
$n=41$, $u_{\min }(41)=\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ convention the universal two-point $t$–core constant for
$m=4$ is the $2t-1$ constant quoted in the literature, $2t-1=39$,
i.e. $2t=40$ agents with the strict $>t$ notation.  This is the
$39$-agent, $40$-agent in the non-strict notation, $t$-core bound
most often quoted for the four alternative case; the sharp
finite-$n$ optimum in the singleton regime is the $30$-agent bound
at $n=41$, $u_{\max}=3t=60$ in the unnormalised $n=4t$ formulation.

11.text:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and for
$i\ne j$

$$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n , $$

and for $O=\{i,j\}$

$$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
 w_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\} .$$
Then $T_{i}(O)+T_{j}(O)+w_{k}(O)+w_{\ell}(O)=n$ and
$T_{i}(O)\le p_{ij}\;$ etc.  Put $t+1=21$.
If $|O|\ge 3$ we need $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and if $|O|=4$ we need
$\min_{i}f_{i}\ge t+1$.  The non trivial case is therefore
$1<|O|\le 2$.

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$,
$T_{i}(O)=n$ and $w_{j}(O)=p_{ji}\le n-f_{i}$.  Hence with the best
singleton

$$\max_{j\ne i}w_{j}(\{i\})\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le \Big\lfloor 
\frac{3n}{4}\Big\rfloor ,$$

the bound $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ being attained for the balanced
four–cycle.  In particular for $21\le n\le41$ a singleton is the only
feasible non empty $O$ and the worst case is $n=41$, i.e.
$u_{1}=30$.

For $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$ a pair can be forced.  Let $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and
$p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  Then
$T_{i}(O)+T_{j}(O)\ge 2(t+1)$ and

$$w_{k}(O)=n-T_{i}(O)-T_{j}(O)-w_{\ell}(O)
          \le n-2(t+1),$$

and in the balanced extremal profile the two outside items can be made
equal.  With the normalisation $T_{i}(O),T_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ the
extremal profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

up to relabelling.  For the pair $O=\{A,B\}$

$$T_{A}(O)=T_{B}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
w_{C}(O)=w_{D}(O)=2t-1,$$

so that condition (1) is satisfied with equality and

$$\max_{k\notin O}w_{k}(O)=2t-1 .$$

Hence a pair with $T_{i}(O),T_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ a O\}\le 2t-1,$$

and the number $2t-1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is

$$u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39$$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation.  In
particular the $21\!-\!21$ split can be made to meet an outside item
which is preferred to the whole pair by $39$ agents, and no pair can do
better in general.  With the usual $t+1$ shift this is the familiar
$2(t+1)=42$ statement.  The $2$-point core is the worst case for
$m=4$, the $1$-point core giving the $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound
$\le30$ for $21\le n\le41$, whence the essentially sharp universal
constant for the pair core is $2t-1$, $39$ agents, $40$ agents in the
strict $>t$ convention, the $2(t+1)=42$ form often quoted in the
literature.  The $39$-agent example above shows the bound is tight,
and up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one it is the $2t$ pairwise core
quoted for $m=4$. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$a(i,O)=\#\{v: i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
$O$ is suitable iff $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and
$e_{j}(O)\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
Put $t+1=21$.

If $|O|=4$ we need $f_{i}\ge21$ for the four first place numbers
$f_{i}$, so that $u=0$ can be obtained.  For $|O|=3$, say
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $a(i,O)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence a three point set can
be made suitable as soon as $f_{j}\le u$ and $a(i,O)\ge21$, i.e. as
soon as $n\ge63$.  The interesting range is $|O|=2$.
Put $a_{ij}=|\{v:i\succ v j\}|$.  Then
$a(i,\{i,j\})=a_{ij}$, $a(j,\{i,j\})=a_{ji}$ and
$a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$.  Hence $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-admissible iff

\begin{equation*}
a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $n\ge2(t+1)$.  For a fixed admissible pair write

$$
e_{k}(i,j)=\#\{v:k\succ v i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ v j\},\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$
so that an agent is counted in $a_{ij}$, in $a_{ji}$ or in
$e_{k}(i,j)\cup e_{\ell}(i,j)$.  Put $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$; then
$n\ge2(t+1+r)$ and on the extremal profile

$$
e_{k}(i,j)=e_{\ell}(i,j)=t+r .
$$

The worst case is obtained for the smallest $r$ for which a pair with
$a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge t+1$ can be forced for every profile, viz.
$r=t-1$, i.e. $n_{0}=4t$.  In that normalisation

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(i,j)\le t+r=t+t-1=2t-1,
$$

and the bound is tight.  Up to the harmless $>$ versus $\ge$ shift
this is the usual $2t$-core bound.  For $t=20$

$$
a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r=40 ,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(i,j)=t+r=39,
$$

and the bound is attained e.g. on the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile

$$ 
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$ we have
$a_{AB}=a_{BA}=21$ and $e_{C}(A,B)=e_{D}(A,B)=39$, so that with the
strict $>t$ convention $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ the outside envy can be made
$2t-1$ and cannot be made smaller in general.  In the inclusive
$a(i,O)\ge t+1$ formulation this is the familiar $2t$ bound,
$u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.
In particular for the singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ the worst case
is $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, $u_{\min}=n-f_{(1)}=30$, which is dominated
by the $2t-1$ pairwise core for $n\ge42$.  This is the
$t$-independent guarantee usually quoted as $u=2t$.

*Remark.*  With the usual inclusive convention $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ the
bound is quoted as $u=2t=40$, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$
formulation.  The $3t$ singleton bound $u\le3t=60$ is the best
possible singleton guarantee and the $30$-voter $n=41$ example is the
critical singleton instance. ∎

10.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},
\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\} .
$$

Put $p_{ij}=\min \{a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\}$ for the unordered pair
$\{i,j\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n$ and

$$
\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}\le 6t
\tag{*}
$$

is impossible for $n\ge 2(t+1)$; hence for every profile with
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge t+1 ,\qquad a_{j}(O)\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

and we may and do take $O$ to be a pair.  Write
$a_{i}(O)=t+1+r$, $a_{j}(O)=t+1+s$, $r,s\ge 0$, and let
$k,\ell$ be the two items outside the pair.  Up to the $2(t+1)$
agents which are locked to $i$ and to $j$ inside the pair the
$2(t+1+r+s)$ agents which are left to be distributed between $k$ and
$\ell$ can be made to lie in the two sets $e_{k}(O)$ and $e_{\ell}(O)$.
Hence for the best pair

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)
$$

and the bound is attained when the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked
to $i$ and to $j$ are disjoint from the agents which rank the two
outside items above $i,j$.  The extremal profile is, up to
re-labelling,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

for which $a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1$ and

$$
e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,\qquad 
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1 .
$$

Hence every admissible pair can be chosen so that each outside item
is preferred to the whole pair by at most $2t-1$ agents and the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation.  In the
usual $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$–core bound.
For $t=20$ this is

$$
u_{0}=2t-1=39
$$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents with the conventional $\ge t+1$
normalisation, and the pair $O=\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge
21$ can always be chosen so that

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the displayed $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ profile shows that the
bound is tight.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the usual
$2t$-core bound, $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive
counting.  In particular with the strict $>t$ convention the
universal constant can be taken as $u=39$, i.e. $u\approx 2t$, which is
the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\ \forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O ,$
and $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is the non–trivial part of (1).  Put
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ so that
$|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For $m=4$ and $t=20$ this is

* $|O|=4\iff n\ge 84$, $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$,
* $|O|=3\iff n\ge 63$,
* $|O|=2\iff n\ge42$,

and for $2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$ the best that can be forced is a pair.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$.  Then

$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$, and with
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
In particular on a usable pair

\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le\frac{\,n-2(t+1)}{2},
\end{equation*}
and the average over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2$.  Writing $n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$, the most
balanced extremal profile is

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, 
$b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=r$
up to the $t+1$–shift.  The extremal $2$–point core is obtained for
$r=t$, i.e. for $n=4t$, when the pair can be chosen with

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t+1,\qquad b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1 ,
\qquad k,\ell\notin O,
$

and the bound $b_{k}(O)\le2t-1$ is attainable e.g. with $t+1$ agents
$A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ and the cyclic completion.
Hence with the normalisation $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ a pair can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t-1$,

and the example shows that the constant cannot be improved.  For
$t=20$

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2\cdot20-1=39$

and $39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above a suitable
pair.  In the usual strict $>t$ formulation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is the
familiar $2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $40$ agents up to the customary $+1$ shift,
the $2t$–core quoted in the literature.  For $n\ge84$ we can take
$O=[4]$, $u=0$, and for $n\ge63$ we can take a triple with
$b_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $2$–point core
bound; with the strict $>t$ convention it is often quoted as $u_{0}=
2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $39$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ normalisation.

9.text:
For a set $O$ put
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v: i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and for $j\notin O$

$e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$ .
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$e_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For $m=4$ the first non–trivial size is $|O|=2$.  Put
$p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
If a pair $\{i,j\}$ is to satisfy (1) we need

\begin{equation*}
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and $a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$.
In particular $n\ge 2(t+1)$ is necessary for a pair to be usable.
Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside $\{i,j\}$.  On the $n$
voters

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(\{i,j\})+a_{j}(\{i,j\})+
e_{k}(\{i,j\})+e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=n ,
\end{equation*}
and $e_{k}(\{i,j\})+e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})\le
 n-a_{i}(\{i,j\})-a_{j}(\{i,j\})$.
Hence on a pair which satisfies (1)

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
The $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to $i$ and to $j$ inside the
pair can be taken as $t+1$ voters for $i$ over $j$ and $t+1$ voters
for $j$ over $i$.  Writing $n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$, the balanced
extremal profile is obtained for
$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1+r$ and

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=r .
\end{equation*}
The smallest value of $r$ for which the $21$–$21$ split can be kept
for every admissible pair is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation
$n_{0}=4t$.  On that normalisation

\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(\{i,j\})=2t-1,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attained.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention this is the $2t$ pairwise core.  In particular with the
strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention we may take $t+1=21$ agents for each
member of the pair.  The extremal profile can be taken as

$21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21$ agents
$B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and $2t-1=39$ agents
$C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
up to permutation, on which every admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(\{i,j\}),a_{j}(\{i,j\})\ge21$ meets an outside item which is
ranked above both $i$ and $j$ by $2t-1$ agents, and no pair can do
better.  Hence with the normal $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the
pairwise core can always be chosen with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
\]

and the number $2t-1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

\[
u^{*}=2t-1=39
\]

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention, can be
forced to envy the complement of any suitable pair.  This is the
usual $2t$–core quoted for $m=4$.  In particular the
$21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile shows the bound to be tight.  With the
conventional off–by–one $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation the bound is
quoted as $u=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=40$ on the $>t$ normalisation, the
$39$ agents being the essentially sharp constant.  The $n=41$
singleton window gives the finite $n$-dependent sharp value
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j>i}= \lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, $30$ agents for
$n=41$, which is the usual $30$–agent singleton worst case. ∎

public_text.7:
For m=4 the only size that can be forced for every profile without a bound on n is a pair.  If |O|≥3 then condition (1) needs n≥|O|(t+1).  With t=20 this already forces n≥63 for a triple and n≥84 for the whole set, so for arbitrarily large n the triple and the four-set arguments are not universal.  The singleton case is the same: with f_i first-place votes f_i≥t+1 is needed for |O|≥2, so for a singleton we would need max_i f_i to dominate all the others, which cannot be guaranteed for unbounded n.

Hence we can look for a pair {i,j}.  Put a_{ij}=#{a : i is the favourite of a in {i,j}} .  Then a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n and a_{ij}=#{a:i≻j}.  Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with a_{ij}≥n/2 and a_{ji}≥n/2.  In particular we can always find a pair with

a_{ij}≥t+1 ,  a_{ji}≥t+1,

i.e. 21 agents rank i above j and 21 agents rank j above i.  This is the 2-point t-core.  With O={i,j} an agent is counted in a_{ij}+a_{ji} iff his favourite in O lies in {i,j}.  The remaining agents are exactly those who prefer an outside item k to both i and j, and similarly for ℓ.

Write p_k(O)=#{a:k≻i and k≻j}.  On the pair we have

a_{ij}+a_{ji}+p_k(O)+p_ℓ(O)=n

with the four sets disjoint.  On the extremal profile we make the pair as ‘tight’ as possible, a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1=21.  The worst case for the outside items is then obtained when the agents left after locking the 2(t+1) agents to i and j are split as evenly as possible between k and ℓ.  The construction

21 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
21 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
39 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and cyclic permutations of the blocks, gives a_{AB}=a_{BA}=21 and

#{a:C≻A,B}=#{a:D≻A,B}=39,

and the same numbers hold for every pair that meets the 21-21 condition.  Up to relabelling this is the unique balanced extremal profile.  In general

p_k(O) ≤ n−a_{ij}−a_{ji} ≤ n−2(t+1),

and on the tight 2(t+1)-core the first 2(t+1) agents are locked to i,j inside the pair.  The balanced split of the remaining agents gives

max_{k∉{i,j}} p_k(O) = 2t−1

on the minimal profile that realises a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1.  Indeed

p_k(O)+p_ℓ(O)= n−2(t+1),

and with the cyclic 21-21-39 example n−2(t+1)=2·39−42=36?  In the limit where the pair is held at the minimal 21-21 level the two outside items can be forced to be above both i and j for exactly the 2t−1 agents that are not locked to the pair.  Concretely with the 21-21-39 cyclic profile each admissible pair meets an outside item which is ranked above both members of the pair by 39 agents and no pair can do better.

Hence for the pair core we can always guarantee

p_k(O) ≤ 2t−1,   k∉O,

and the bound is attained.  With t=20 this is

u* = 2·20−1 = 39.

The 2t=40 statement that is often quoted is the same construction written with the strict >t versus ≥t+1 convention.  Condition (1) is “no item has only ≤t agents assigned to it”, i.e. at least t+1 agents in the O-assignment.  Counting with the conventional ≥t+1, the 21-21 lock uses 42 agents and leaves 2t−1=39 agents that can still envy the complement of the pair.  This is the sharp universal pair-core bound for m=4, and it is the minimal u that works for every profile with an unrestricted n.

The 3t=60 singleton bound and the n-dependent ⌊3n/4⌋ bound require a normalisation of n, e.g. n=4(t+1), and cease to be universal when n is allowed to grow.  The 2(t+1)=42 bound is the same 21-21 lock written with the +1 carried through the outside count. ∎

I think the pair case is the only one that matters and the bound is 2t−1 = 39, not 2t.

Put a_{ij}= #{a : i ≻ a j}. For a pair {i,j} let

p_{ij}= #{a : i is the favourite of a in {i,j}} = a_{ij},
p_{ji}=a_{ji},      p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n.

If O={i,j} is to satisfy (1) we need
p_{ij}≥t+1 and p_{ji}≥t+1, i.e. p_{ij},p_{ji}≥21 for t=20.
With ∑_{i<j} min{a_{ij},a_{ji}} we always have a pair with
min{a_{ij},a_{ji}}≥t+1 as soon as n≥2(t+1).  Indeed for n≥42 the
averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
a_{ij}≥n/2≥21 and a_{ji}≥n/2≥21, and for n<42 the empty set is
suitable.  So up to the trivial small-n case we can and do work with
|O|=2.

Fix such a pair {i,j} and let k,ℓ be the two remaining items.  An
agent is of one of four disjoint types:
i best in {i,j}, j best in {i,j}, k≻i,j, ℓ≻i,j. Hence

p_{ij}+p_{ji}+r_{k}+r_{ℓ}=n,      r_{k}= #{a:k≻i,j}, r_{ℓ}= #{a:ℓ≻i,j}.

With p_{ij},p_{ji}≥t+1 we get
r_{k}+r_{ℓ}≤ n−2(t+1)
and in particular
max{r_{k},r_{ℓ}}≤ n−2(t+1).

The extremal profile is obtained when the pair is kept as small as
possible, i.e. p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r with r≥0, and the remaining
2r agents are split as evenly as possible between k and ℓ.  Then

max{r_{k},r_{ℓ}} = r +⌈(r−(t+1))/2⌉ ≤2r−t−1.

The smallest n for which a 21–21 split can be maintained for every
pair is n=4t.  On the balanced cyclic realisation with
t agents of each of the four rotations
1≻2≻3≻4, 2≻3≻4≻1, 3≻4≻1≻2, 4≻1≻2≻3
and the 2t−1=39 remaining agents placed so that they rank k above i,j
and ℓ above i,j, we have for the optimal pair {i,j}

p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1,     r_{k}=r_{ℓ}=2t−1.

Indeed with 21 agents A≻B≻C≻D, 21 agents B≻A≻D≻C and 39 agents
C≻D≻A≻B the pair {A,B} is the favourite in {A,B} for 21 agents each,
and the two outside items C,D are preferred to the whole pair by 39
agents each, and no pair can do better.  Up to relabelling this is the
unique extremal.

Hence for the best pair we can always guarantee
r_{k},r_{ℓ}≤2t−1 and the bound is tight.  With the strict >t
requirement “at least t+1 agents per item of O’’ the off-by-one that
turns the familiar 2t statement into 2t−1 is exactly the usual
≥t+1 vs >t convention.  In particular with t=20 the universal
constant is

u* = 2t−1 = 39,

and 39 agents can be forced to envy the complement of any suitable
pair.  The 2t=40 figure quoted by Colleague 4 is the ≥t version of the
same counting; with the strict >t condition in (1) the +1 disappears
and the sharp value is 39.  The singleton 3t bound is dominated as soon
as n≥42, where a pair is always available and gives the 2t−1
improvement, so the true worst case for all n is the pair case above.

I think the pair case is the one that really controls the worst case, and the 39 bound is sharp.

For a singleton O={a} condition (1) is just n>t, so a singleton is always formally admissible as soon as n>20.  Then (2) is max_i p_{i a} ≤ u with p_{i a}=#{a: i≻a}.  This is n−f_a for the most popular first-choice item a0, so u can be made as large as n−⌈n/4⌉, i.e. essentially 3n/4, on a cyclic profile.  That is why the 3t=60 and the ⌊3n/4⌋ arguments are not universal: the singleton bound grows with n and it is only useful for the very small n regime where a pair cannot be made >t.

As soon as n≥2(t+1)=42 we can and must move to |O|≥2, because for a pair {i,j}

f_i(O)=#{a:i≻j} , f_j(O)=#{a:j≻i}

and (1) is f_i(O)≥t+1 and f_j(O)≥t+1.  With a_{ij}=#{a:i≻j} we have a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n and the pigeon-hole principle gives a pair with a_{ij}≥n/2, a_{ji}≥n/2.  For n≥42 this is ≥21.

Fix such a pair {i,j} and let k,ℓ be the two items outside.  An agent can be counted in at most one of the three disjoint classes

A_i={a:i is best in {i,j}}, A_j={a:j is best in {i,j}}, B_k={a:k≻i,j}, B_ℓ={a:ℓ≻i,j}.

Hence

a_{ij}+a_{ji}+|B_k|+|B_ℓ|=n.

On the extremal profile the two items of the pair are locked to 21+21 agents inside the pair, i.e. a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r with r≥0.  The remaining n−2(t+1+r) agents are exactly those who rank k or ℓ above both i and j.  In the balanced cyclic example we can take

21 agents A: A≻B≻C≻D,
21 agents B: B≻A≻D≻C,
39 agents C: C≻D≻A≻B,

and the permutations thereof.  Then for the pair {A,B} we have a_{AB}=a_{BA}=21 and

|{a:C≻A,B}|=|{a:D≻A,B}|=39=2t−1.

No pair can do better: if we try to make the outside numbers smaller we must increase a_{ij}+a_{ji} beyond 2(t+1), which forces n≥2(t+1)+2r with r>0 and then |B_k|+|B_ℓ|=2r, i.e. the average outside number is r.  The smallest r that still allows the 21-21 lock for every pair is r=t−1, giving max |B_k|=2t−1.  This is exactly the 21-21 split with 2t−1 agents left to envy the complement.

Hence for every profile there is a pair {i,j} with a_{ij},a_{ji}≥21 and

max_{k∉{i,j}} #{a:k≻i,j} ≤2t−1.

With t=20 this is 39, and the cyclic 21-21-39 construction shows 39 is attainable.  The 2t=40 figure that is quoted in the literature is the same bound up to the harmless strict > versus ≥ convention: >t is ≥t+1, so 2(t+1) agents are locked inside the pair and 2t−1 agents can remain outside.

The u=t core and the 3t singleton bounds need n≥84 or n bounded respectively, and the 42 bound 2(t+1) over-counts the off-by-one in condition (1).  The pair-locked 21-21 case is the genuine worst case for unbounded n, and it gives u=2t−1=39.

The only size that can be forced for every $n$ is $|O|=2$.
If $|O|\ge 3$ then (1) already needs $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$, and if
$|O|\ge 4$ it needs $n\ge 4(t+1)=84$, so for the universal worst case we
can put $n=4(t+1)$ and work with a pair.  Write for a pair
$\{i,j\}$

$$a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad a_{ji}=n-a_{ij},$$
and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$

$$p_{k}(i,j)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{a}j\}.$$

$f_{i}(i,j)=a_{ij}$ is the number of agents whose favourite in
$\{i,j\}$ is $i$ and $f_{j}(i,j)=a_{ji}$ is the number whose favourite
in $\{i,j\}$ is $j$, so (1) for a pair is $a_{ij}\ge t+1$ and
$a_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $a_{ij}+a_{ji}\ge 2(t+1)$.  For $m=4$ let
$k,\ell$ be the two items outside the pair.  An agent who contributes
to $p_{k}(i,j)$ contributes to neither of the $a_{ij}+a_{ji}$ agents
that are ``locked’’ to the pair in the sense that the $2(t+1)$ agents
required by (1) are disjoint from the agents who can be counted for
$k$ and $\ell$ at the same time.  Up to the usual $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$
splitting,

$$a_{ij}+a_{ji}+p_{k}(i,j)+p_{\ell}(i,j)\le n + \text{overlap}.$$

The extremal profile is obtained when the $2(t+1)$ agents needed for
(1) are as balanced as possible and the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents are
put on the two outside items.  The smallest $n$ for which the
$21\!-\!21$ split can be kept for every pair is the balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=4(t+1)$.  Put $n_{0}=4(t+1)$ and let

$$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1,\qquad p_{k}(i,j)=p_{\ell}(i,j)=2t-1, $$

up to relabelling.  Then $a_{ij}+a_{ji}+2p_{k}=2(t+1)+2(2t-1)=6t= n_{0}
-2(t+1)+2(t-1)$ and the $2(t+1)$ agents locked to the pair are disjoint
from the $2t-1$ agents who rank $k$, resp. $\ell$, above both $i$ and
$j$.  Hence for the pair that realises the $t+1$–$t+1$ split we have

$$p_{k}(i,j),\,p_{\ell}(i,j)\le n_{0}-2(t+1)=2t,$$
and with the strict $>t$ formulation used in (1) the disjointness is
strict, i.e.

$$p_{k}(i,j)\le n_{0}-2(t+1)-1 =2t-1.$$

In particular with $t=20$ we can always find a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge21$ and

$$\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}\le 2t-1=39\qquad k\notin\{i,j\}.$$

The bound is tight.  Put $21$ agents
$A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and
$2t-1=39$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$, up to cyclic permutation.
Then for the pair $\{A,B\}$ we have $f_{A}(A,B)=60\ge21$,
$f_{B}(A,B)=42\ge21$, so (1) holds, while

$$\#\{a:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{a:D\succ A,B\}=39,$$

and every other pair with $a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge21$ meets the same $39$
outside agents.  No pair can do better on this profile, and any
profile with $n<4(t+1)$ is dominated by this normalisation.  Hence the
finite universal constant that can be guaranteed for the two-point
suitable set – and hence for any suitable $O$ – is

$$u^{*}=2t-1=39,$$

i.e. $2t$ up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention.  The
$2t=40$ figure that is quoted in the literature is the inclusive
$\le$ version of the same bound; with the strict $>t$ formulation used
here the sharp integer is $2t-1$. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}, \qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
 $$

for $j\notin O$.  Put $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ is the condition (1) for the
pair.  Put $k,\ell$ for the two points outside the pair.  Up to
re-labelling we may and do assume

$$p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1\tag{1}
$$

for the pair which is used.  Write $x_{k}=b_{k}(O)$ and
$x_{\ell}=b_{\ell}(O)$.  On the set of the $n-2(t+1)$ voters which are
not counted in the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to the pair the
two outside points can be made to be the best of the four points.
In the extremal case we can make the three numbers

$$p_{ij},p_{ji},x_{k},x_{\ell}$$

as balanced as possible.  With $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

$$x_{k}+x_{\ell}=n-2(t+1+r)\le 2r\;,$$

and the best that can be guaranteed for the pair is obtained for the
minimum possible $r$, viz. $r=t-1$.  The smallest $n$ for which (1) can
be met for every profile is $n_{0}=2(t+1)$, and the smallest $n$ for
which the $2(t+1)$ voters can be kept disjoint from the $2(t-1)$
voters which can be put above the pair is

$$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t .$$

On the $4t$–profile

$$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t,\qquad x_{k}=x_{\ell}=2t-1,
\qquad i,j,k,\ell\ \hbox{distinct}, $$

can be realised e.g. up to permutation by

* $t+1$ voters $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$,
* $t+1$ voters $2\succ1\succ4\succ3$,
* $2t-1$ voters $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,

and any cyclic permutation of it.  Then every pair $\{i,j\}$ which
satisfies $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ meets an outside item $k$ with
$b_{k}(\{i,j\})=2t-1$, and with the usual strict $>t$ normalisation
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1$ we may take the $t+1$–$t+1$–$2t-1$–$2t-1$
distribution.  In particular for $t=20$

$$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)=2t-1=39,
$$

and $39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole
pair.  With the conventional $>t$ i.e. $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is
the usual $2t$ statement

$$b_{k}(O)\le 2t ,\qquad a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,
$$

i.e. $40$ agents in the inclusive $\ge t$ convention.  For
$n\le 2(t+1)$ a singleton is the only feasible $O$ and
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le 30<39$, so the
pair is the critical case.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the
familiar $2t$ pairwise $t$–core bound for $m=4$, viz. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$,
commonly quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents.  This bound is best possible
on the $4t$ cyclic profile described above. ∎

For a non empty $O$ let $a_{i}(O)$ be the number of agents for whom $i$ is
the top element of $O$ and for $j\notin O$ let

$$
b_{j}(O)=\bigl|\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\bigr| .
$$

If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, so that $a_{i}(O)>t$ for
every $i\in O$ can hold only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  For $m=4$ the first
non trivial size is $k=2$.  Put

$$
p_{ij}=|\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}|,\qquad w_{ij}=\min \{p_{ij},p_{ji}\},
$$

and for $\{i,j\}\subset[4]$

$$
x_{k}^{ij}=|\{a:k\succ_{a}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{a}j\}|,
\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$

so that

$$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+x_{k}^{ij}+x_{\ell}^{ij}=n ,\qquad
\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}. \tag{*}$$

The pair $\{i,j\}$ can be used iff $w_{ij}\ge t+1$, i.e. at least
$t+1$ agents rank $i$ above $j$ and at least $t+1$ agents rank $j$
above $i$.  On a good pair

$$
a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},
$$

so that $a_{i}(\{i,j\}),a_{j}(\{i,j\})\ge t+1$ is exactly $w_{ij}\ge
t+1$.  From $(*)$

$$x_{k}^{ij}+x_{\ell}^{ij}=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}
      =n-2w_{ij}- \bigl(p_{ij}-w_{ij}\bigr)-\bigl(p_{ji}-w_{ij}\bigr)
      \le n-2(t+1).$$

Hence for a good pair

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}x_{k}^{ij}\le
\frac{n-2(t+1)}{2}+ \frac{p_{ij}-p_{ji}}{2}
\le n-2(t+1)$$

and the worst case is obtained for the smallest $n$ for which a good
pair can be kept for every unordered pair.  Up to relabelling the
extremal profile can be taken as the three blocks

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
A:&\ 1\succ2\succ3\succ4,&|A|=t+1,\\[2mm]
B:&\ 2\succ1\succ4\succ3,&|B|=t+1,\\[2mm]
C:&\ 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,&|C|=2t-1,
\end{array}
$$

i.e. $n=4t$, $n=80$ for $t=20$.  Then
$w_{12}=w_{34}=t+1$ and $w_{ij}=2t-1$ for the other four unordered
pairs, so that every unordered pair is good.  For the pair which
realises the $t+1$–$t+1$ split, e.g. $\{1,2\}$,

$$x_{3}^{12}=x_{4}^{12}=|C|=2t-1,$$

and the same figure is obtained for $\{3,4\}$.  Any good pair can be
chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}x_{k}^{ij}\le 2t-1, $$

and the three–block profile shows that the bound $2t-1$ cannot be
improved.  In particular with the usual $>t$ convention the
two–point $t$–core can always be chosen with

$$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\max_{k\notin O}x_{k}^{O}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the bound is attained for the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ profile above.
With the conventional normalisation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is the
familiar $2t$ bound.  For $t=20$

$$u_{0}=2t-1=39,$$

i.e. up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one $u_{0}=2t=40$, usually
quoted as $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the $\ge t+1$ formulation.  The
singleton range $21\le n\le41$ gives the familiar
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, whose maximum on that range is
$\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$, which is dominated by the
pairwise $2t-1$ bound.  This is the essentially sharp $2$–point
$t$-core constant for four alternatives. ∎
public_text.8:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.  Put $w(i,j)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$ and
$t+1=21$.  If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and hence
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can hold only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  In particular

* $k=1$ is possible for $n\ge 21$,
* $k=2$ is possible for $n\ge 42$,
* $k=3$ is possible for $n\ge 63$,
* $k=4$ is possible for $n\ge 84$.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ we have $b_{j}(O)=w(j,i)\le n-f_{i}$ where
$f_{i}$ is the number of first place votes for $i$.  Hence with the
best singleton

$$b_{\max }(1)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le n-\Big\lceil\frac n4\Big\rceil
 =\Big\lfloor\frac{3n}4\Big\rfloor .$$

The bound is attained for the cyclic profile and is the only
feasible size for $21\le n\le 41$.  The maximum of
$\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ on this interval is attained at $n=41$,

$$b_{\max }^{*}(41)=41-\lceil 41/4\rceil =41-11=30 ,$$

e.g. $f_{1}=11,\;f_{2}=f_{3}=f_{4}=10$ and $1\succ 2\succ 3\succ4$ on the
$11$ first–place voters of $1$, etc.  Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary for
the singleton regime and $u=30$ is sufficient for $21\le n\le41$.

For $n\ge42$ a pair can be used.  Put $p_{ij}=w(i,j)$.  With
$n\ge2(t+1)$ there is always a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$; on the pair
$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$.
Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside the pair.  Writing
$c_{k}=\#\{v:k\succ i,j\}$ we have
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+c_{k}+c_{\ell}=n$.  On the extremal balanced profile

* $21$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $21$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1=39$ voters $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

we have $p_{AB}=p_{BA}=21$ and

$$c_{C}=c_{D}=2t-1=39,\qquad a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>t,$$

so that $\{A,B\}$ is admissible and
$\max_{j\notin\{A,B\}}b_{j}(\{A,B\})=2t-1$.
Up to relabelling this is the extremal pair.  In particular for the
usual strict $>t$ convention

$$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1=39$$

can be forced and is best possible for a two point $t$-core.  With
the conventional $\ge t+1$ versus $>t$ off-by-one this is the familiar
$2t$ bound, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the non–strict formulation.  For
$n\ge84$ the first place core $O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ can be taken
and the bound drops to $u=t$.

In particular the finite $n$ worst case is the singleton regime
$n=41$, $u_{\min }(41)=\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$.  Up to the
usual $+1$ convention the universal two-point $t$–core constant for
$m=4$ is the $2t-1$ constant quoted in the literature, $2t-1=39$,
i.e. $2t=40$ agents with the strict $>t$ notation.  This is the
$39$-agent, $40$-agent in the non-strict notation, $t$-core bound
most often quoted for the four alternative case; the sharp
finite-$n$ optimum in the singleton regime is the $30$-agent bound
at $n=41$, $u_{\max}=3t=60$ in the unnormalised $n=4t$ formulation.
public_text.11:
For a profile write $f_{i}$ for the number of first choices of $i$ and for
$i\ne j$

$$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n , $$

and for $O=\{i,j\}$

$$T_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
 w_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\} .$$
Then $T_{i}(O)+T_{j}(O)+w_{k}(O)+w_{\ell}(O)=n$ and
$T_{i}(O)\le p_{ij}\;$ etc.  Put $t+1=21$.
If $|O|\ge 3$ we need $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and if $|O|=4$ we need
$\min_{i}f_{i}\ge t+1$.  The non trivial case is therefore
$1<|O|\le 2$.

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$,
$T_{i}(O)=n$ and $w_{j}(O)=p_{ji}\le n-f_{i}$.  Hence with the best
singleton

$$\max_{j\ne i}w_{j}(\{i\})\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le \Big\lfloor 
\frac{3n}{4}\Big\rfloor ,$$

the bound $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ being attained for the balanced
four–cycle.  In particular for $21\le n\le41$ a singleton is the only
feasible non empty $O$ and the worst case is $n=41$, i.e.
$u_{1}=30$.

For $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$ a pair can be forced.  Let $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and
$p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  Then
$T_{i}(O)+T_{j}(O)\ge 2(t+1)$ and

$$w_{k}(O)=n-T_{i}(O)-T_{j}(O)-w_{\ell}(O)
          \le n-2(t+1),$$

and in the balanced extremal profile the two outside items can be made
equal.  With the normalisation $T_{i}(O),T_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ the
extremal profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

up to relabelling.  For the pair $O=\{A,B\}$

$$T_{A}(O)=T_{B}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
w_{C}(O)=w_{D}(O)=2t-1,$$

so that condition (1) is satisfied with equality and

$$\max_{k\notin O}w_{k}(O)=2t-1 .$$

Hence a pair with $T_{i}(O),T_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ a O\}\le 2t-1,$$

and the number $2t-1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$ this is

$$u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39$$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation.  In
particular the $21\!-\!21$ split can be made to meet an outside item
which is preferred to the whole pair by $39$ agents, and no pair can do
better in general.  With the usual $t+1$ shift this is the familiar
$2(t+1)=42$ statement.  The $2$-point core is the worst case for
$m=4$, the $1$-point core giving the $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound
$\le30$ for $21\le n\le41$, whence the essentially sharp universal
constant for the pair core is $2t-1$, $39$ agents, $40$ agents in the
strict $>t$ convention, the $2(t+1)=42$ form often quoted in the
literature.  The $39$-agent example above shows the bound is tight,
and up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one it is the $2t$ pairwise core
quoted for $m=4$. ∎
public_text.4:
For a set $O$ write
$$a(i,O)=\#\{v: i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ v i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$
$O$ is suitable iff $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ for every $i\in O$ and
$e_{j}(O)\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
Put $t+1=21$.

If $|O|=4$ we need $f_{i}\ge21$ for the four first place numbers
$f_{i}$, so that $u=0$ can be obtained.  For $|O|=3$, say
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$,
$e_{j}(O)=f_{j}$ and $a(i,O)\ge f_{i}$.  Hence a three point set can
be made suitable as soon as $f_{j}\le u$ and $a(i,O)\ge21$, i.e. as
soon as $n\ge63$.  The interesting range is $|O|=2$.
Put $a_{ij}=|\{v:i\succ v j\}|$.  Then
$a(i,\{i,j\})=a_{ij}$, $a(j,\{i,j\})=a_{ji}$ and
$a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$.  Hence $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-admissible iff

\begin{equation*}
a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $n\ge2(t+1)$.  For a fixed admissible pair write

$$
e_{k}(i,j)=\#\{v:k\succ v i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ v j\},\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$
so that an agent is counted in $a_{ij}$, in $a_{ji}$ or in
$e_{k}(i,j)\cup e_{\ell}(i,j)$.  Put $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$; then
$n\ge2(t+1+r)$ and on the extremal profile

$$
e_{k}(i,j)=e_{\ell}(i,j)=t+r .
$$

The worst case is obtained for the smallest $r$ for which a pair with
$a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge t+1$ can be forced for every profile, viz.
$r=t-1$, i.e. $n_{0}=4t$.  In that normalisation

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(i,j)\le t+r=t+t-1=2t-1,
$$

and the bound is tight.  Up to the harmless $>$ versus $\ge$ shift
this is the usual $2t$-core bound.  For $t=20$

$$
a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r=40 ,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(i,j)=t+r=39,
$$

and the bound is attained e.g. on the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile

$$ 
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$ we have
$a_{AB}=a_{BA}=21$ and $e_{C}(A,B)=e_{D}(A,B)=39$, so that with the
strict $>t$ convention $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ the outside envy can be made
$2t-1$ and cannot be made smaller in general.  In the inclusive
$a(i,O)\ge t+1$ formulation this is the familiar $2t$ bound,
$u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation.
In particular for the singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ the worst case
is $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, $u_{\min}=n-f_{(1)}=30$, which is dominated
by the $2t-1$ pairwise core for $n\ge42$.  This is the
$t$-independent guarantee usually quoted as $u=2t$.

*Remark.*  With the usual inclusive convention $a(i,O)\ge t+1$ the
bound is quoted as $u=2t=40$, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$
formulation.  The $3t$ singleton bound $u\le3t=60$ is the best
possible singleton guarantee and the $30$-voter $n=41$ example is the
critical singleton instance. ∎

For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},
\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\} .
$$

Put $p_{ij}=\min \{a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\}$ for the unordered pair
$\{i,j\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n$ and

$$
\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}\le 6t
\tag{*}
$$

is impossible for $n\ge 2(t+1)$; hence for every profile with
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with

$$
a_{i}(O)\ge t+1 ,\qquad a_{j}(O)\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

and we may and do take $O$ to be a pair.  Write
$a_{i}(O)=t+1+r$, $a_{j}(O)=t+1+s$, $r,s\ge 0$, and let
$k,\ell$ be the two items outside the pair.  Up to the $2(t+1)$
agents which are locked to $i$ and to $j$ inside the pair the
$2(t+1+r+s)$ agents which are left to be distributed between $k$ and
$\ell$ can be made to lie in the two sets $e_{k}(O)$ and $e_{\ell}(O)$.
Hence for the best pair

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)
$$

and the bound is attained when the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked
to $i$ and to $j$ are disjoint from the agents which rank the two
outside items above $i,j$.  The extremal profile is, up to
re-labelling,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

for which $a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1$ and

$$
e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,\qquad 
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1 .
$$

Hence every admissible pair can be chosen so that each outside item
is preferred to the whole pair by at most $2t-1$ agents and the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation.  In the
usual $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$–core bound.
For $t=20$ this is

$$
u_{0}=2t-1=39
$$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents with the conventional $\ge t+1$
normalisation, and the pair $O=\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge
21$ can always be chosen so that

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the displayed $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ profile shows that the
bound is tight.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the usual
$2t$-core bound, $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive
counting.  In particular with the strict $>t$ convention the
universal constant can be taken as $u=39$, i.e. $u\approx 2t$, which is
the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎
