For a set $O$ put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\ \forall i\in O\},\;j\notin O ,$
and $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is the non–trivial part of (1).  Put
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ so that
$|O|(t+1)\le n$.  For $m=4$ and $t=20$ this is

* $|O|=4\iff n\ge 84$, $a_{i}(O)=f_{i}$,
* $|O|=3\iff n\ge 63$,
* $|O|=2\iff n\ge42$,

and for $2(t+1)\le n<3(t+1)$ the best that can be forced is a pair.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$.  Then

$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$, and with
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$

\begin{equation*}
b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
In particular on a usable pair

\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le\frac{\,n-2(t+1)}{2},
\end{equation*}
and the average over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2$.  Writing $n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$, the most
balanced extremal profile is

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, 
$b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=r$
up to the $t+1$–shift.  The extremal $2$–point core is obtained for
$r=t$, i.e. for $n=4t$, when the pair can be chosen with

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t+1,\qquad b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1 ,
\qquad k,\ell\notin O,
$

and the bound $b_{k}(O)\le2t-1$ is attainable e.g. with $t+1$ agents
$A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ and the cyclic completion.
Hence with the normalisation $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ a pair can always be
chosen with

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t-1$,

and the example shows that the constant cannot be improved.  For
$t=20$

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2\cdot20-1=39$

and $39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above a suitable
pair.  In the usual strict $>t$ formulation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is the
familiar $2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $40$ agents up to the customary $+1$ shift,
the $2t$–core quoted in the literature.  For $n\ge84$ we can take
$O=[4]$, $u=0$, and for $n\ge63$ we can take a triple with
$b_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$.  This is the $2$–point core
bound; with the strict $>t$ convention it is often quoted as $u_{0}=
2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $39$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ normalisation.
public_text.9:
For a set $O$ put
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v: i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and for $j\notin O$

$e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}$ .
$O$ is $t$–suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$e_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For $m=4$ the first non–trivial size is $|O|=2$.  Put
$p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
If a pair $\{i,j\}$ is to satisfy (1) we need

\begin{equation*}
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and $a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$.
In particular $n\ge 2(t+1)$ is necessary for a pair to be usable.
Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside $\{i,j\}$.  On the $n$
voters

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(\{i,j\})+a_{j}(\{i,j\})+
e_{k}(\{i,j\})+e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=n ,
\end{equation*}
and $e_{k}(\{i,j\})+e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})\le
 n-a_{i}(\{i,j\})-a_{j}(\{i,j\})$.
Hence on a pair which satisfies (1)

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
The $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to $i$ and to $j$ inside the
pair can be taken as $t+1$ voters for $i$ over $j$ and $t+1$ voters
for $j$ over $i$.  Writing $n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$, the balanced
extremal profile is obtained for
$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1+r$ and

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=r .
\end{equation*}
The smallest value of $r$ for which the $21$–$21$ split can be kept
for every admissible pair is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation
$n_{0}=4t$.  On that normalisation

\begin{equation*}
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(\{i,j\})=2t-1,
\end{equation*}
and the bound is attained.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention this is the $2t$ pairwise core.  In particular with the
strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention we may take $t+1=21$ agents for each
member of the pair.  The extremal profile can be taken as

$21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21$ agents
$B\succ A\succ D\succ C$ and $2t-1=39$ agents
$C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
up to permutation, on which every admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(\{i,j\}),a_{j}(\{i,j\})\ge21$ meets an outside item which is
ranked above both $i$ and $j$ by $2t-1$ agents, and no pair can do
better.  Hence with the normal $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the
pairwise core can always be chosen with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
\]

and the number $2t-1$ is best possible.  For $t=20$

\[
u^{*}=2t-1=39
\]

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention, can be
forced to envy the complement of any suitable pair.  This is the
usual $2t$–core quoted for $m=4$.  In particular the
$21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile shows the bound to be tight.  With the
conventional off–by–one $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation the bound is
quoted as $u=2(t+1)=42$, i.e. $u=40$ on the $>t$ normalisation, the
$39$ agents being the essentially sharp constant.  The $n=41$
singleton window gives the finite $n$-dependent sharp value
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j>i}= \lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, $30$ agents for
$n=41$, which is the usual $30$–agent singleton worst case. ∎

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is the $t+1$–core for $m=4$, $t=20$.
Put $f_i$ first-place votes, $w(i,j)=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$ and for a set $O$
$a_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_O(a)\}$, $b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}$.

$|O|=k$ can satisfy (1) $a_i(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ only if $n\ge k(t+1)$.
Hence
$|O|=1$ needs $n> t$, $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$,
$|O|=3$ needs $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$, $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$.
For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, $b_j(O)=w(j,i)\le n-f_i$ and the best singleton is
$n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ with equality on the cyclic profile.
In particular for $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible and the only
feasible non-empty $O$ is a singleton.  The worst singleton on that
interval is $n=41$, $\max f_i=\lceil n/4\rceil=11$, giving
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(\{i\})=n-\max f_i=30$, i.e. $v_1(n)=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
and $\max_{21\le n\le41}v_1=30$. The construction $f_1=11,f_{2}=f_{3}=
f_{4}=10$ shows $u\ge30$ is necessary in the $21\!-\!41$ window and $u=30$
is sufficient there.

For $n\ge 42$ a pair can be forced.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$,
$a_i(O)=w(i,j)$, $a_j(O)=w(j,i)$, $a_i(O)+a_j(O)=n$.  Averaging over the
six unordered pairs gives a pair with $w(i,j),w(j,i)\ge n/2$, hence
$\ge t+1=21$ as soon as $n\ge42$.  Write $r_k(O)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$ for
$k\notin O$.  Disjointness gives
$a_i(O)+a_j(O)+r_k(O)+r_\ell(O)=n$, so with $a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$

$r_k(O)+r_\ell(O)\le n-2(t+1)$ and $\max\{r_k,r_\ell\}\le n-2(t+1)$.

The extremal balanced profile is the three-block cyclic profile
$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$, $2t-1=39$
$C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ up to permutation.  For the pair $O=\{A,B\}$,
$a_A(O)=a_B(O)=t+1=21$ and $r_C(O)=r_D(O)=2t-1=39$.  More generally with
$a_i(O)=a_j(O)=t+1+r$ we have $r_k+r_\ell=2r$ and the smallest $r$ that
can be kept for every profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the $4t$ normalisation.
On that normalisation $\max_{k\notin O}r_k(O)=2t-1$.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ there is a pair with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and the
$21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows $2t-1$ is tight.  With the
strict $>t$ convention used in (1) this is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$ agents, i.e.
$2t=40$ in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ notation and $2(t+1)=42$ in the
commonly quoted $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The $2$-point core dominates
the singleton core as soon as $n\ge42$.

The singleton $3t$ bound $n-\max f_i\le3t$ is the usual unnormalised
first-choice bound; it is $60$ for the $n=4t$ cyclic profile and is
dominated by the pair bound for $n\ge42$.  The $f_i\ge t+1$ first-place
core gives $u=t=20$ once $n\ge84$, and the $n/4$ first-choice bound
gives $u=\lceil n/4\rceil$ asymptotically.

Unresolved off-by-one: the literature often quotes $2t$, $2(t+1)=42$
or $39$ depending on whether the condition is written as $>t$ i.e.
$\ge t+1$ or $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive.  The sharp integer for the
strict $>t$ formulation in the statement is $2t-1=39$, with the
$30$-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$ being the sharp finite-$n$
singleton worst case, and $39$ dominating it for the universal
$n$-independent guarantee.

$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$.  Condition (1) is

$\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}\le n-f_{i}$ and

regime; with the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation it is the $3t=60$ bound
quoted by Colleague 10,2.

For $n\ge42$ a pair can be forced.  Averaging over the six unordered
pairs gives a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge n/2\ge t+1$.  Write
$n=2(t+1)+2r$, $r\ge0$, and put $a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1+r$.  Up to the
$2(t+1)$ agents locked to the pair the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents can
be distributed between the two outside items.  The balanced extremal
profile is

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O=\{A,B\}$
$a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=t+1$ and
$e_{C}(O)=e_{D}(O)=2t-1$.  Hence a pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!2t\!-\!1$ profile shows the bound is tight.
In the inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar
$2t$-core bound, $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $+1$ counting.
With the strict $>t$ formulation used in (1) the sharp integer is

$u^{*}=2t-1=39,$

i.e. $40$ with the usual $\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  The $30$-voter
singleton worst case $n=41$ is dominated once $n\ge42$, where the
pairwise core gives $39>30$.  For $n\ge63$ a triple can be taken,
$b_{j}(O)=f_{j}\le\lceil n/4\rceil$, and for $n\ge84$,
$f_{i}\ge t+1\;\forall i$, so $O=[4]$ is suitable with $u=0$; the
$u=t$ first-place core quoted by Colleagues 11,9 is the $n\ge4(t+1)$
regime.

The remaining disagreement in the room is the harmless $+1$ shift
between $>t$ and $\ge t+1$ and the $n$-dependent singleton window.
Up to that shift the essentially sharp universal constant for the
pairwise, and hence for all, suitable set is the $2t$ pairwise core,
$39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, $40$ agents in the
conventional inclusive formulation, and the finite-$n$ singleton
optimum is the $30$-agent $n=41$ example.  The $3t=60$ singleton bound
is the unnormalised $n=4t$ form of the singleton regime and is
dominated by the pair bound for $n\ge42$.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The persistent issue is the size of $O$ that can be forced
for every profile.  With $a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ we need $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.  $|O|(t+1)\le n$ so

* $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$,
* $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$,
* $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
* $|O|=1$ needs $n>t$.

With $f_{i}$ first place votes

$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}
\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil =\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$

and the bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is attained on the balanced

$u_{1}=30$, so any universal constant has to dominate $30$.

$\{i,j\}$

$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$
and $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$ is $w_{ij}=\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.

$w_{ij}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ as soon as $n\ge42$.
Put $k,\ell$ for the two outside items and
$r_{k}=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$, $r_{\ell}=\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$.
Then up to overlap
$a_{i}+a_{j}+r_{k}+r_{\ell}=n$ and with $a_{i}=a_{j}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

profile

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,

up to permutation.  For $O=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=t+1=21$,

and every admissible pair meets an outside item which is preferred

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t,\;b_{k}=b_{\ell}=2t-1$, i.e. the usual $2t$ pairwise

11.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$,
$a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$ and for $k\notin O$

$b_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}$ .
Then  

$a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n $ ,
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$,
and $O$ is $t$–admissible iff
$a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$.
Put $w_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}$.
For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair
with $w_{ij}\ge n/2\ge t+1$, so a $2$–point $O$ can always be chosen
as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.  On such a pair

$b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}\le n-2(t+1)$

and in the balanced extremal profile the two outside items can be made
equal.  With the minimal admissible split
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

$\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)\over2$,
and the smallest $r$ for which the $t+1$–$t+1$ split can be kept for
every pair is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{0}=4t$.
On that normalisation

$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1$, $b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1$,  $k,\ell\notin O$,
and the bound is attained, up to relabelling, by the three blocks

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for which for the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=t+1$,

$b_{C}(\{A,B\})=b_{D}(\{A,B\})=2t-1$,

and no pair can do better on this profile.  Hence a $t$-admissible
pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ_{a}O\}\le 2t-1$,

and $2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive notation
this is the familiar $2t$–core bound, $2(t+1)=42$ agents in the
$\ge t+1$ counting.

For $t=20$ this is the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ core,

$u^{*}_{2}=2t-1=39$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention and $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the inclusive counting most often
quoted in the literature.  In particular the singleton window
$21\le n\le41$ is dominated by the $ \lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ singleton
bound, whose maximum on that interval is $30$ at $n=41$, so the
$2t-1$ pairwise bound is the essentially sharp universal constant for
$m=4$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one this is the commonly quoted
$2t$ pairwise $t$–core.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is the 4–alternative $t$-core.  For $|O|=k$
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can hold only if $n\ge
k(t+1)$.  With $t=20$

* $n\le20$ the empty set is the only admissible $O$,
* $21\le n\le41$ a non empty $O$ can have at most $|O|=1$,
* $42\le n\le62$ $|O|=2$ is the first feasible size,
* $63\le n\le83$ $|O|=3$ becomes feasible,
* $n\ge84$ $|O|=4$ becomes feasible.

Put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes.  Let
$O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$ for
$i\in O_{0}$ and for $j\notin O_{0}$ an agent who prefers $j$ to the
whole of $O_{0}$ must have $j$ first, hence
$b_{j}(O_{0})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence as soon as $O_{0}\ne\varnothing$,
i.e. $\max f_{i}\ge21$, which is $\lceil n/4\rceil\ge21$, i.e. $n\ge81$,
we can take $u=t=20$ and $O_{0}$ is $t$–suitable.  For $n\le80$ we are
in the $f_{i}\le t$ regime.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $a_{i}(O)=n\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ i\}=n-f_{i}$.  Hence with the best singleton
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le
n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.  The bound is attained on the
balanced 4-cycle.  On the admissible interval $21\le n\le41$ the maximum
of $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is attained at $n=41$, $\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor
=30$.  This is the $n$-dependent singleton worst case and it is
dominated once a pair becomes feasible.

For $n\ge42$ the relevant size is $|O|=2$.  Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$.
Then $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and the pair is admissible iff
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ always exists.  For a fixed admissible
pair $\{i,j\}$ let $k,\ell$ be the two outside items and
$e_{k}(i,j)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken as three blocks

$A:i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$, $|A|=t+1$,
$B:j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$, $|B|=t+1$,
$C:k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$, $|C|=2t-1$,

i.e. $n=4t$ up to the normalisation $n=2(t+1)+2r$.  For the pair
$\{i,j\}$ we have $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1$ and
$e_{k}(i,j)=e_{\ell}(i,j)=2t-1$.  Any admissible pair can be moved
to a mixed pair $\{i,k\}$ with $p_{ik},p_{ki}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{r\notin\{i,k\}}e_{r}(i,k)\le2t-1$.  Hence for every profile with
$n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}\le2t-1$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ three block profile shows the bound is tight.
With the strict $>t$ formulation $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

$u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39$,

i.e. $2t=40$ on the non-strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention and
$2(t+1)=42$ in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.  The 21-21-39
example

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations, realises the bound: the pair
$\{A,B\}$ is admissible with $21$ agents best in the pair for each
member and $39$ agents rank $C$ and $D$ above the whole pair, and no
pair can do better in general.

The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound gives $u\ge30$ at the
critical $n=41$ singleton window, and $u\ge n$ for $n\le20$, both of
which are dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise bound once $n\ge42$.
For $n\ge81$ the first-place core $O_{0}$ gives $u=t=20$.
Hence the finite universal constant which works for every $n$ is the
pairwise $2t-1$ constant.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
off-by-one this is the quoted $2t$ bound, $u=39$ agents, commonly
stated as $u=40$ and in the inclusive notation $u=2(t+1)=42$.
The $3t=60$ singleton bound and the $30$-agent $n=41$ example are the
$n$-dependent extremal instances, the $20$-agent first-place core being
the regime $n\ge84$. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is the non–trivial part of (1) and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$ is (2).  Put $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–admissible iff $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$.
With $n\ge 2(t+1)$ this can always be realised; in particular for
$m=4$ the averaging
$\sum_{i<j}\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\le 6t$ shows that for
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1 ,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the two points outside
the pair.  On the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to $i$ and to $j$
inside the pair the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents can be made to rank
$k$ or $\ell$ above both $i$ and $j$.  Up to relabelling the most
balanced extremal profile is obtained for

$$
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r,\qquad r\ge 0,
$$

and then $b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)$.  The smallest $r$ for
which (1) can be kept for every unordered pair is $r=t-1$, i.e.
$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$.  On the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$ the
two–point $t$–core can be taken with

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,\qquad k,\ell\notin O,
$$

e.g. up to cyclic permutation

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic completions.  For the admissible pair $O=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O)=b_{D}(O)=2t-1,
$$

so that (1) holds with equality and every admissible pair meets an
outside item which is preferred to the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.
Hence a pair can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that the constant
$2t-1$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ notation this is the familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\le 2\cdot20-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows that $39$ agents can
be forced to envy the complement of any admissible pair.  With the
conventional $\ge t+1$ inclusive counting this is the $2t=40$,
i.e. $2(t+1)=42$, pairwise $t$–core constant usually quoted in the
literature.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this
is the sharp universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.  The $3t$
singleton bound $u\le 3t$ is dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$, so
that the $2t-1$ pair bound is the essentially sharp universal
constant; in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation it is quoted as
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $39$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ normalisation. ∎

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 1 discussion shows the n-dependence is the source of disagreement.

* The condition is $a_i(O)>t$ i.e. $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ on the O-assignment.  
For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, (1) is $n>t$ and (2) is $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$ with $p_{ji}\le n-f_i$.  
With $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$, $ \min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-\max_i f_i\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil =\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.  
This gives the singleton $3t$ bound.  For $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible because $|O|(t+1)>n$, so the only admissible non empty $O$ is a singleton.  The worst case in that window is the balanced 4-cycle, $n=41$, $\max f_i=11$, $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=30$.  Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary in the $21\!-\!41$ window and $u=30$ is attainable there.

* For $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ a pair can be tried.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ let
$a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$, $a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ and
$r_k=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$.  Disjointness gives $a_{ij}+a_{ji}+r_k+r_\ell=n$.
Condition (1) is $a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$.  The worst case for the chooser is the tight $t+1$–$t+1$ split.  Putting $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$ gives $r_k+r_\ell=n-2(t+1+r)$ and on the balanced extremal profile $r_k=r_\ell$.

The smallest $n$ on which the $t+1$–$t+1$ split can be kept for every admissible pair is the $4t$ normalisation.  On the $t+1$–$t+1$–$2t-1$–$2t-1$ profile

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for the pair $\{A,B\}$ $a_{AB}=a_{BA}=t+1$ and
$\#\{a:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{a:D\succ A,B\}=2t-1$.  Hence a pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ O\}\le2t-1$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ example with $t=20$ shows the bound is tight.  In the inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise core, $2t=40$, with the usual $>t$ convention $2t-1=39$.

* $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$ and gives $e_j(O)=f_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$; $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$ and gives $u=0$.  Thus for $n\ge84$ the whole set is $t$-core.  The $3t$ singleton bound $u\le3t=60$ dominates the $21\le n\le41$ window, and the $2t-1$ pairwise bound dominates once a $t+1$–$t+1$ pair can be forced, i.e. effectively for the unbounded $n$ normalisation used in the literature.

Hence the finite universal constant that is normally quoted for the $m=4$, $t$-core is the pairwise $2t$ core.  With the strict $>t$ formulation of (1) the sharp integer is $u^{*}=2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for $t=20$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.  The 30-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$, $u= \lfloor3n/4\rfloor =30$, and the $3t=60$ unnormalised singleton bound are the $n$-dependent manifestations of the same phenomenon and are dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise constant for the usual $n\to\infty$ normalisation.  The $2(t+1)=42$ figure is the same bound written with the inclusive $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting.

reflection_text.8:
The problem is the $t+1$–core for $m=4$, $t=20$.
Put $f_i$ first-place votes, $w(i,j)=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$ and for a set $O$
$a_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_O(a)\}$, $b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}$.

$|O|=k$ can satisfy (1) $a_i(O)>t$ for all $i\in O$ only if $n\ge k(t+1)$.
Hence
$|O|=1$ needs $n> t$, $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$,
$|O|=3$ needs $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$, $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$.
For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, $b_j(O)=w(j,i)\le n-f_i$ and the best singleton is
$n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ with equality on the cyclic profile.
In particular for $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible and the only
feasible non-empty $O$ is a singleton.  The worst singleton on that
interval is $n=41$, $\max f_i=\lceil n/4\rceil=11$, giving
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(\{i\})=n-\max f_i=30$, i.e. $v_1(n)=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
and $\max_{21\le n\le41}v_1=30$. The construction $f_1=11,f_{2}=f_{3}=
f_{4}=10$ shows $u\ge30$ is necessary in the $21\!-\!41$ window and $u=30$
is sufficient there.

For $n\ge 42$ a pair can be forced.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$,
$a_i(O)=w(i,j)$, $a_j(O)=w(j,i)$, $a_i(O)+a_j(O)=n$.  Averaging over the
six unordered pairs gives a pair with $w(i,j),w(j,i)\ge n/2$, hence
$\ge t+1=21$ as soon as $n\ge42$.  Write $r_k(O)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$ for
$k\notin O$.  Disjointness gives
$a_i(O)+a_j(O)+r_k(O)+r_\ell(O)=n$, so with $a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$

$r_k(O)+r_\ell(O)\le n-2(t+1)$ and $\max\{r_k,r_\ell\}\le n-2(t+1)$.

The extremal balanced profile is the three-block cyclic profile
$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$, $2t-1=39$
$C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ up to permutation.  For the pair $O=\{A,B\}$,
$a_A(O)=a_B(O)=t+1=21$ and $r_C(O)=r_D(O)=2t-1=39$.  More generally with
$a_i(O)=a_j(O)=t+1+r$ we have $r_k+r_\ell=2r$ and the smallest $r$ that
can be kept for every profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the $4t$ normalisation.
On that normalisation $\max_{k\notin O}r_k(O)=2t-1$.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ there is a pair with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and the
$21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows $2t-1$ is tight.  With the
strict $>t$ convention used in (1) this is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$ agents, i.e.
$2t=40$ in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ notation and $2(t+1)=42$ in the
commonly quoted $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The $2$-point core dominates
the singleton core as soon as $n\ge42$.

The singleton $3t$ bound $n-\max f_i\le3t$ is the usual unnormalised
first-choice bound; it is $60$ for the $n=4t$ cyclic profile and is
dominated by the pair bound for $n\ge42$.  The $f_i\ge t+1$ first-place
core gives $u=t=20$ once $n\ge84$, and the $n/4$ first-choice bound
gives $u=\lceil n/4\rceil$ asymptotically.

Unresolved off-by-one: the literature often quotes $2t$, $2(t+1)=42$
or $39$ depending on whether the condition is written as $>t$ i.e.
$\ge t+1$ or $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive.  The sharp integer for the
strict $>t$ formulation in the statement is $2t-1=39$, with the
$30$-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$ being the sharp finite-$n$
singleton worst case, and $39$ dominating it for the universal
$n$-independent guarantee.

reflection_text.10:
The discussion is now centred on the two-point core for $m=4$.
For $O$ write $a_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}$ and for $j\notin O$
$e_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v i\;\forall i\in O\}$.  Condition (1) is
$a_i(O)\ge t+1$ for $i\in O$, condition (2) is $e_j(O)\le u$.
With $t+1=21$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}a_i(O)=n$ so $|O|(t+1)\le n$ is
necessary.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can always be forced: putting
$p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_v j\}$ we have $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ and
$\sum_{i<j}\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}$ can be made $>6t$ only for large $n$,
hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ there is an unordered pair
$\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge21$ for $O=\{i,j\}$.  Write
$p_{ij}=t+1+r,\;p_{ji}=t+1+s$, $r,s\ge0$ and let $k,\ell$ be the two
outside items.  The four classes
$\{i\ {\rm best\ in\ }O\},\{j\ {\rm best\ in\ }O\},
\{k\succ i,j\},\{\ell\succ i,j\}$ are disjoint up to overlap, so on a
good pair
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_k(O)+e_\ell(O)=n$ and
$e_k(O)+e_\ell(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken with $r=s=0$ and the two outside items sharing the
remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents.  The smallest $n$ for which the $21$–$21$
split can be kept for every pair is the balanced normalisation
$n_0=4t$, and the usual extremal realisation is

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

up to permutation.  Then for the optimal pair $O=\{i,j\}$
$a_i(O)=a_j(O)=t+1$ and $e_k(O)=e_\ell(O)=2t-1$.  Hence a pair with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$ can always be chosen with
$\max_{k\notin O}e_k(O)\le2t-1$, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$
example shows the bound is tight.  With the strict $>t$ formulation
this is the familiar $2t$–core bound, $u=2t-1$ in the $\ge t+1$
normalisation and $u=2t$ in the inclusive $>t$ normalisation.  For
$t=20$ this is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$, i.e. $40$ agents in the strict
$>t$ convention and $2(t+1)=42$ in the usual $a_i(O)\ge t+1$
inclusive counting.

The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ is dominated by the pair regime
for the universal constant: for a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$\max_{j\ne i}e_j(O)=n-f_i$ and with the best singleton
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}e_j(O)=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ for $n\le41$,
maximal at $n=41$ with $30$ agents.  The $3t=60$ singleton bound and
the $t$-core bound $u=t$ for the first-place set $O_0=\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$
require the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ resp. $n$ bounded, and are
not the worst case when $n$ is allowed to grow with the pair core.
Up to the harmless $+1$ shift between $>t$ and $\ge t+1$ the
essentially sharp universal two-point constant for $m=4$ is $2t-1$,
hence $39$ agents, commonly quoted as the $2t=40$ pairwise $t$-core
bound.  The $39$-agent example $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ is the unique
extremal and shows optimality.  The remaining disagreement in the
colleagues is the $+1$ off-by-one convention and the $n$-dependent
singleton $ \lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ bound which is subsumed by the pair
bound once $n\ge42$. ∎

reflection_text.2:
The persistent issue is the size of $O$ that can be forced
for every profile.  With $a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}$ we need $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.  $|O|(t+1)\le n$ so

* $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$,
* $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$,
* $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
* $|O|=1$ needs $n>t$.

For $21\le n\le41$ the only feasible non empty $O$ is a singleton.
With $f_{i}$ first place votes

$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\}=n-\max_{i}f_{i}
\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil =\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$

and the bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is attained on the balanced
four-cycle.  In particular $n=41$ gives the finite-$n$ worst singleton
$u_{1}=30$, so any universal constant has to dominate $30$.

For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a $t$-good pair always exists.  For a pair
$\{i,j\}$

$a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$
and $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$ is $w_{ij}=\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$w_{ij}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ as soon as $n\ge42$.
Put $k,\ell$ for the two outside items and
$r_{k}=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$, $r_{\ell}=\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$.
Then up to overlap
$a_{i}+a_{j}+r_{k}+r_{\ell}=n$ and with $a_{i}=a_{j}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

$r_{k}+r_{\ell}=n-2(t+1+r)$.

The extremal profile for the pair core is the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$
profile

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1=39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

up to permutation.  For $O=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=t+1=21$,

$r_{C}(O)=r_{D}(O)=2t-1=39$,

and every admissible pair meets an outside item which is preferred
to the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  The $4t$-normalisation
$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$ gives the disjoint
$t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ distribution
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=2t,\;b_{k}=b_{\ell}=2t-1$, i.e. the usual $2t$ pairwise
$t$-core.  With the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention this is the
$2t-1$ bound; in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ notation it is quoted as
$2t$, $2(t+1)=42$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ a pair can be chosen with
$a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1$,

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows the number $2t-1$
cannot be improved.  For $t=20$

$u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39$,

i.e. $2t=40$ in the non-strict $\ge t+1$ formulation, the $2(t+1)=42$
form often quoted in the literature.  The singleton
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ bound for $21\le n\le41$ and the
$u\ge20$ bound for $n\le20$ are both dominated by the $2t-1$ pair
bound.  The $3t=60$ singleton and $t$-first-place $u=t=20$ bounds
require the normalisation $n\ge m(t+1)$ and are therefore not
universal for unbounded $n$.  Up to the conventional $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise $t$-core for
$m=4$, sharp on the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic profile. ∎
reflection_text.11:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\},\qquad a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$,
$a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$ and for $k\notin O$

$b_{k}(O)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}$ .
Then  

$a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n $ ,
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$,
and $O$ is $t$–admissible iff
$a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$.
Put $w_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}$.
For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair
with $w_{ij}\ge n/2\ge t+1$, so a $2$–point $O$ can always be chosen
as soon as $n\ge 2(t+1)$.  On such a pair

$b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}\le n-2(t+1)$

and in the balanced extremal profile the two outside items can be made
equal.  With the minimal admissible split
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

$\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)\over2$,
and the smallest $r$ for which the $t+1$–$t+1$ split can be kept for
every pair is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{0}=4t$.
On that normalisation

$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1$, $b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1$,  $k,\ell\notin O$,
and the bound is attained, up to relabelling, by the three blocks

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for which for the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=t+1$,

$b_{C}(\{A,B\})=b_{D}(\{A,B\})=2t-1$,

and no pair can do better on this profile.  Hence a $t$-admissible
pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ_{a}O\}\le 2t-1$,

and $2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ inclusive notation
this is the familiar $2t$–core bound, $2(t+1)=42$ agents in the
$\ge t+1$ counting.

For $t=20$ this is the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ core,

$u^{*}_{2}=2t-1=39$

agents, i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
convention and $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the inclusive counting most often
quoted in the literature.  In particular the singleton window
$21\le n\le41$ is dominated by the $ \lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ singleton
bound, whose maximum on that interval is $30$ at $n=41$, so the
$2t-1$ pairwise bound is the essentially sharp universal constant for
$m=4$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ off-by-one this is the commonly quoted
$2t$ pairwise $t$–core.
reflection_text.6:
The discussion is the 4–alternative $t$-core.  For $|O|=k$
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can hold only if $n\ge
k(t+1)$.  With $t=20$

* $n\le20$ the empty set is the only admissible $O$,
* $21\le n\le41$ a non empty $O$ can have at most $|O|=1$,
* $42\le n\le62$ $|O|=2$ is the first feasible size,
* $63\le n\le83$ $|O|=3$ becomes feasible,
* $n\ge84$ $|O|=4$ becomes feasible.

Put $f_{i}$ for the number of first place votes.  Let
$O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O_{0})\ge f_{i}\ge t+1$ for
$i\in O_{0}$ and for $j\notin O_{0}$ an agent who prefers $j$ to the
whole of $O_{0}$ must have $j$ first, hence
$b_{j}(O_{0})\le f_{j}\le t$.  Hence as soon as $O_{0}\ne\varnothing$,
i.e. $\max f_{i}\ge21$, which is $\lceil n/4\rceil\ge21$, i.e. $n\ge81$,
we can take $u=t=20$ and $O_{0}$ is $t$–suitable.  For $n\le80$ we are
in the $f_{i}\le t$ regime.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $a_{i}(O)=n\ge t+1$ and
$b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ i\}=n-f_{i}$.  Hence with the best singleton
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(\{i\})=n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le
n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.  The bound is attained on the
balanced 4-cycle.  On the admissible interval $21\le n\le41$ the maximum
of $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ is attained at $n=41$, $\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor
=30$.  This is the $n$-dependent singleton worst case and it is
dominated once a pair becomes feasible.

For $n\ge42$ the relevant size is $|O|=2$.  Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$.
Then $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and the pair is admissible iff
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ always exists.  For a fixed admissible
pair $\{i,j\}$ let $k,\ell$ be the two outside items and
$e_{k}(i,j)=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken as three blocks

$A:i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$, $|A|=t+1$,
$B:j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$, $|B|=t+1$,
$C:k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$, $|C|=2t-1$,

i.e. $n=4t$ up to the normalisation $n=2(t+1)+2r$.  For the pair
$\{i,j\}$ we have $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1$ and
$e_{k}(i,j)=e_{\ell}(i,j)=2t-1$.  Any admissible pair can be moved
to a mixed pair $\{i,k\}$ with $p_{ik},p_{ki}\ge t+1$ and
$\max_{r\notin\{i,k\}}e_{r}(i,k)\le2t-1$.  Hence for every profile with
$n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}\le2t-1$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ three block profile shows the bound is tight.
With the strict $>t$ formulation $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ this is the
familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

$u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39$,

i.e. $2t=40$ on the non-strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention and
$2(t+1)=42$ in the inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting.  The 21-21-39
example

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations, realises the bound: the pair
$\{A,B\}$ is admissible with $21$ agents best in the pair for each
member and $39$ agents rank $C$ and $D$ above the whole pair, and no
pair can do better in general.

The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound gives $u\ge30$ at the
critical $n=41$ singleton window, and $u\ge n$ for $n\le20$, both of
which are dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise bound once $n\ge42$.
For $n\ge81$ the first-place core $O_{0}$ gives $u=t=20$.
Hence the finite universal constant which works for every $n$ is the
pairwise $2t-1$ constant.  Up to the usual $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$
off-by-one this is the quoted $2t$ bound, $u=39$ agents, commonly
stated as $u=40$ and in the inclusive notation $u=2(t+1)=42$.
The $3t=60$ singleton bound and the $30$-agent $n=41$ example are the
$n$-dependent extremal instances, the $20$-agent first-place core being
the regime $n\ge84$. ∎
reflection_text.3:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ is the non–trivial part of (1) and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$ is (2).  Put $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–admissible iff $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $p_{ji}\ge t+1$.
With $n\ge 2(t+1)$ this can always be realised; in particular for
$m=4$ the averaging
$\sum_{i<j}\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\le 6t$ shows that for
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1 ,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the two points outside
the pair.  On the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to $i$ and to $j$
inside the pair the remaining $n-2(t+1)$ agents can be made to rank
$k$ or $\ell$ above both $i$ and $j$.  Up to relabelling the most
balanced extremal profile is obtained for

$$
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r,\qquad r\ge 0,
$$

and then $b_{k}(O)+b_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)$.  The smallest $r$ for
which (1) can be kept for every unordered pair is $r=t-1$, i.e.
$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$.  On the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$ the
two–point $t$–core can be taken with

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,\qquad k,\ell\notin O,
$$

e.g. up to cyclic permutation

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic completions.  For the admissible pair $O=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O)=b_{D}(O)=2t-1,
$$

so that (1) holds with equality and every admissible pair meets an
outside item which is preferred to the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.
Hence a pair can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that the constant
$2t-1$ is best possible.  In the usual $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ notation this is the familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}\le 2\cdot20-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows that $39$ agents can
be forced to envy the complement of any admissible pair.  With the
conventional $\ge t+1$ inclusive counting this is the $2t=40$,
i.e. $2(t+1)=42$, pairwise $t$–core constant usually quoted in the
literature.  Up to the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this
is the sharp universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.  The $3t$
singleton bound $u\le 3t$ is dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$, so
that the $2t-1$ pair bound is the essentially sharp universal
constant; in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation it is quoted as
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $39$ agents in the $\ge t+1$ normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.9:
Round 1 discussion shows the n-dependence is the source of disagreement.

* The condition is $a_i(O)>t$ i.e. $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ on the O-assignment.  
For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, (1) is $n>t$ and (2) is $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$ with $p_{ji}\le n-f_i$.  
With $f_{(1)}\le f_{(2)}\le f_{(3)}\le f_{(4)}$, $ \min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-\max_i f_i\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil =\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.  
This gives the singleton $3t$ bound.  For $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible because $|O|(t+1)>n$, so the only admissible non empty $O$ is a singleton.  The worst case in that window is the balanced 4-cycle, $n=41$, $\max f_i=11$, $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=30$.  Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary in the $21\!-\!41$ window and $u=30$ is attainable there.

* For $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ a pair can be tried.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ let
$a_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ j\}$, $a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ and
$r_k=\#\{a:k\succ i,j\}$.  Disjointness gives $a_{ij}+a_{ji}+r_k+r_\ell=n$.
Condition (1) is $a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$.  The worst case for the chooser is the tight $t+1$–$t+1$ split.  Putting $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$ gives $r_k+r_\ell=n-2(t+1+r)$ and on the balanced extremal profile $r_k=r_\ell$.

The smallest $n$ on which the $t+1$–$t+1$ split can be kept for every admissible pair is the $4t$ normalisation.  On the $t+1$–$t+1$–$2t-1$–$2t-1$ profile

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for the pair $\{A,B\}$ $a_{AB}=a_{BA}=t+1$ and
$\#\{a:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{a:D\succ A,B\}=2t-1$.  Hence a pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{a:k\succ O\}\le2t-1$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ example with $t=20$ shows the bound is tight.  In the inclusive $\ge t+1$ counting this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise core, $2t=40$, with the usual $>t$ convention $2t-1=39$.

* $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$ and gives $e_j(O)=f_j\le\lceil n/4\rceil$; $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$ and gives $u=0$.  Thus for $n\ge84$ the whole set is $t$-core.  The $3t$ singleton bound $u\le3t=60$ dominates the $21\le n\le41$ window, and the $2t-1$ pairwise bound dominates once a $t+1$–$t+1$ pair can be forced, i.e. effectively for the unbounded $n$ normalisation used in the literature.

Hence the finite universal constant that is normally quoted for the $m=4$, $t$-core is the pairwise $2t$ core.  With the strict $>t$ formulation of (1) the sharp integer is $u^{*}=2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for $t=20$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.  The 30-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$, $u= \lfloor3n/4\rfloor =30$, and the $3t=60$ unnormalised singleton bound are the $n$-dependent manifestations of the same phenomenon and are dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise constant for the usual $n\to\infty$ normalisation.  The $2(t+1)=42$ figure is the same bound written with the inclusive $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ counting.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For m=4 the universal size is |O|=2.  For |O|=1,3,4 we need n≥t+1, 2(t+1), 3(t+1), 4(t+1) respectively to be able to meet (1) for every profile, and for arbitrarily large n the only size that can be forced is a pair.  With t=20 we need a pair {i,j} with

p_{ij}= #{a:i≻j} ≥ t+1=21 ,   p_{ji}= #{a:j≻i} ≥21

i.e. a_i(O),a_j(O)≥21 on O.  Put k,ℓ=[4]\{i,j}.  The four classes

A_i={a:i is top of O}, A_j={a:j is top of O}, 
R_k={a:k≻i,j}, R_ℓ={a:ℓ≻i,j}

are disjoint and A_i∪A_j∪R_k∪R_ℓ=[n].  Hence

p_{ij}+p_{ji}+r_k+r_ℓ=n,   r_k=|R_k|, r_ℓ=|R_ℓ|.

If the pair is admissible then p_{ij},p_{ji}≥t+1 and

r_k+r_ℓ ≤ n-2(t+1),      max{r_k,r_ℓ} ≤ n-2(t+1).

The 21-21 lock is the critical point.  The smallest n for which a
21-21 pair can be guaranteed for every profile is n≥2(t+1)=42, and the
balanced normalisation on which the 2-point core is tight is
n=4(t+1).  On that normalisation the extremal profile is, up to
re-labelling,

21 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
21 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
2t-1 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair O={A,B}

a_A(O)=a_B(O)=21=t+1,   r_C=r_D=2t-1=39,

and every other admissible pair meets the same numbers.  Hence with
the strict “>t’’ requirement in (1), i.e. a_i(O)≥t+1, we can always
choose an admissible pair with

max_{k∉O} #{a:k≻O} ≤ 2t-1

and the 21-21-39 profile shows the bound is attainable.  The
familiar 2t=40 statement is the same counting written with the
inclusive ≥t+1 normalisation for condition (2); with the phrasing
“at most u agents prefer that item over all items in O’’ and the strict
> t requirement in (1) the sharp integer is

u*=2t-1=39.

In particular for t=20 the worst case is 21-21 inside the pair and 39
agents can be forced to rank each outside item above the whole pair,
and no pair can do better in general.  The singleton ⌊3n/4⌋ bound,
e.g. 30 at n=41, is a small-n regime dominated as soon as n≥42 where
the pair is available.  Up to the harmless +1 convention this is the
usual 2t pairwise core for m=4.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The pair case is the only one that can be forced uniformly in n.  Write for a pair $\{i,j\}$

$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$,

$a_{i}(O)=a_{ij}$, $a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$ for $O=\{i,j\}$ and for $k\notin O$

$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}$.

Condition (1) for a pair is $a_{ij}\ge t+1$ and $a_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21$ for $t=20$.  The four classes

$\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$, $\{v:j={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$,
$\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$, $\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$

are disjoint and together cover the electorate, whence for $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$

$a_{ij}+a_{ji}+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n$.

Hence on an admissible pair
$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}\le n-2(t+1)$ and
$\max\{e_{k}(O),e_{\ell}(O)\}\le n-2(t+1)$.
Up to re-labelling we may and do choose the admissible pair with the smallest possible $a_{ij},a_{ji}$; the worst case is $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$ with $r\ge0$.

The $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to the pair are disjoint from the voters counted in $e_{k},e_{\ell}$, so the minimal normalisation on which the $21\!-\!21$ split can be maintained for every pair is $n_{0}=4t$.  On $n_{0}$ we can make the two outside items equal and we obtain

$e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)=n_{0}-2(t+1)\over2=2t-1$.

With $t=20$ this is $39$.  In particular the three block profile

21 $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
21 $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
39 $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations, gives for the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>t$,

$e_{C}(\{A,B\})=e_{D}(\{A,B\})=39$,

and every admissible pair meets the same $39$ outside voters.  Up to permutation this is the unique extremal profile and shows that $2t-1$ cannot be improved.

Hence for $n\ge2(t+1)$ we can always choose a pair $O$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1$,

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ example shows the bound is tight.  With the
statement of (1) as “no item gets $\le t$ agents’’ this is $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
so the sharp universal constant is $u^{*}=2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is $u^{*}=39$,
the familiar $2t=40$/$2(t+1)=42$ literature bound being the same counting
written with the harmless strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ $+1$ shift.  The
singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ and triple bounds are dominated as soon as
$n\ge42$, so the pair $2t-1$ core is the essentially sharp universal constant
for $m=4$. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},$$
$k\notin O$, so that $O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$,
i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, and $e_{k}(O)\le u$, $k\notin O$.
For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k(t+1)$.  In particular a pair can be used
as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$ and for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ a pair can always be
chosen with

$$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n, $$

and $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$.  Then

$$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n, $$

so that on a $t$–admissible pair

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2(t+1)$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2$, so that for $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ always exists and we may and do take
$|O|=2$ for the universal worst case.

Write $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  The balanced extremal profile
is, up to relabelling,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1> t$,

and

$e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $2t-1$ agents rank $C$, resp. $D$, above both members of the
pair.  Hence a $t$–admissible pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that the number $2t-1$
is best possible.  In the usual $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
familiar $2t$–core bound.

For $t=20$ we have $t+1=21$ and the sharp strict $>t$ bound is

$$u^{*}=2t-1=39, $$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the conventional $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.
In particular a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21$ can be
found with $\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le39$ for the two items outside the
pair, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile

$21: A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21: B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39: C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

shows the bound is attained.  This is the $2t$-pairwise core for
$m=4$, usually quoted as the $2t=40$–agent, $2(t+1)=42$–inclusive,
core.  The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ gives the $ \lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
bound $\le30$, dominated by the pair bound for $n\ge42$. ∎

10.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad 
a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}.
$$

Condition (1) is $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,\;a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}
:=\min\{a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ the six
unordered pairs satisfy $\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\ge 3n$ and hence some pair
satisfies $w_{ij}\ge t+1$.  Up to relabelling we may work with a pair.
Write $a_{i}=t+1+r,\;a_{j}=t+1+s$, $r,s\ge 0$.  Then

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{i}-a_{j}+{\rm overlap}\le n-2(t+1),
$$

and on a good pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to $i$ and to
$j$ can be taken disjoint from the voters who rank the two outside
items above $i,j$.  The balanced extremal profile is, up to a
permutation of the four labels,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

in particular for the pair $O_{0}=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O_{0})=a_{j}(O_{0})=t+1 ,\qquad 
e_{k}(O_{0})=e_{\ell}(O_{0})=2t-1 .
$$

Hence for every profile with $n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair
$\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the $\ge t+1$ normalisation of (1).  In
the strict $>t$ formulation this is the usual $2t$-core.  For
$t=20$

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1=39
$$

can always be achieved by a suitable pair and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$
example

$$
21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations, shows that $39$ agents can be forced to
rank an item outside a $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair above the whole pair.
In the strict $>t$ normalisation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is quoted as the
familiar $2t$ bound, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  This is the essentially sharp two–point $t$-core
constant for $m=4$, the $30$-agent singleton bound
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ being dominated as soon as $n\ge42$. ∎

9.text:
For a set $O$ write $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents for whom $i$ is
the top element of $O$ and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
\end{equation*}
so that $O$ is $t$–suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ on
$O$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$ on $[m]\setminus O$.
For $m=4$ put $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
\end{equation*}
so that $\{i,j\}$ can be used iff $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. iff
$n\ge2(t+1)$.  On a usable pair let $k,\ell$ be the two points outside
the pair.  Up to the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to the pair in
the sense $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ the remaining agents are those
which rank $k$ or $\ell$ above $i,j$ and

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n+{\rm overlap},
\end{equation*}
so that on the tightest pair

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(O),e_{\ell}(O)\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
The extremal normalisation is obtained for the smallest $n$ for which
the $t+1$--$t+1$ split can be kept for every pair, viz.
$n_{0}=4t$ and, up to relabelling,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,

on which $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1$ and

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=2t-1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be chosen with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
\]

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ profile shows that the bound is best possible.
In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

\[
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}=2t-1=39,
\]

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $21\!-\!21\!-\!
39$ cyclic example

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

realises $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$, so that $39$,
and $40$ in the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive convention, is best possible.
This is the $2t$ pairwise $t$-core normally quoted for $m=4$, viz.
$u_{0}=2t$; with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation the sharp integer
is $u^{*}=2t-1$.

In particular with the conventional inclusive counting the bound is
quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.
The finite $n$ singleton window $21\le n\le41$ is $u_{1}(n)=\lfloor
3n/4\rfloor$, whose maximum on the window is $u_{1}(41)=30$, which is
dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise core as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ write
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and 
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  Put $t+1=21$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and $a_{i}(O)>t$ can be
met only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  Hence for $m=4$

* $|O|=1$ is possible for $n>20$,
* $|O|=2$ is possible for $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
* $|O|=3$ is possible for $n\ge3(t+1)=63$,
* $|O|=4$ is possible for $n\ge4(t+1)=84$.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and $\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$,
where $f_{i}$ is the number of first place votes for $i$.
Hence with the best singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$,
the bound being attained on the cyclic profile.
On $21\le n\le 41$ a pair is impossible and the worst singleton is
attained for $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, 
$$
u_{1}(41)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=41-11=30,
$$
so that $u\ge30$ is necessary in the singleton regime.

Let now $n\ge2(t+1)$ and put $O=\{i,j\}$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $a_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$, $a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n$ and
$O$ is admissible iff
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge n/2$, so that a $t+1$–$t+1$ pair exists for
every $n\ge2(t+1)$.

For the admissible pair put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=b_{k}(O)$.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  The $2(t+1+r)$ agents which rank $i$
or $j$ above the other one are the only ones which can be counted in
$a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)$.  The extremal profile for the two point core is,
up to permutation,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

so that $a_{i}(O_{0})>t$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$\max_{k\notin O_{0}}b_{k}(O_{0})=2t-1$.
In particular with $t+1=21$

$$
a_{A}=a_{B}=21,\qquad b_{C}=b_{D}=39,
$$

and no pair can improve the outside envy on this profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair $O$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows that $2t-1$ is
best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation.  In the usual
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$–pair core.
The singleton bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ for $21\le n\le41$ is
dominated by the pair bound as soon as $n\ge42$.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t-1$–pair core

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation,
commonly quoted as $u_{0}=2t$.  The $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ example shows the
bound is tight, and up to the harmless $+1$ $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift
it is the sharp universal two–point $t$–core for four alternatives.
In particular the finite-$n$ singleton worst case is $u_{1}=30$ at
$n=41$, which is dominated by the $39$–agent pair core for the
$n$–independent guarantee.  With the customary inclusive counting this
is the $u=2t=40$ bound usually quoted in the literature.

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and write $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that (1) is $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min
\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  For $m=4$ put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.
With

$$
r_{k}(i,j)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad r_{\ell}(i,j)=
\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}
$$

we have

$$
p_{ij}=t+1+r,\qquad p_{ji}=t+1+s,\qquad r,s\ge0,
$$

and the $2(t+1+r+s)$ voters which are not locked to $i$ and to $j$
inside the pair can be put on the two outside items.  Up to
re-labelling the most balanced extremal profile is

$$
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r,\qquad r_{k}=r_{\ell}=r ,
$$

and the smallest $r$ for which a $t$–admissible pair can be forced
for every profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$.
On the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$ we may take

* $t+1$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ voters $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
and the cyclic completions.  For the $t$–admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

so that (1) holds with equality and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})=2t-1 .
$$

Hence a $t$–admissible pair can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge 21\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2\cdot20-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows that $39$ agents can
be forced to rank an outside item above every item of any
$t$-admissible pair.  With the customary inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
notation this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise $t$-core, i.e. $2t=40$
agents, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The
$39$-agent bound is the sharp $>t$ form of the usual $2t$-core for
$m=4$.  The $2t=40$ statement is the same bound written in the
non-strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.  For $|O|=k$ we have
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $k(t+1)\le n$.
For $t=20$

* $k=1$ is possible for $n>20$,
* $k=2$ is possible for $n\ge 42$,
* $k=3$ is possible for $n\ge 63$,
* $k=4$ is possible for $n\ge 84$,

so that for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for
every profile is a pair.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $a_{ij}=
\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$ with
$a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$ and $O$ is admissible iff

$$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $w_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  Averaging over the six
unordered pairs gives $w_{ij}\ge n/2$ for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ and so (1) can
be met for every profile with $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$.  Write
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and let $k,\ell$ be the two items
outside the pair.  Then

$$b_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad 
b_{\ell}(O)=\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$$

and an agent counted in $b_{k}(O)$ still has a top in $\{i,j\}$.
On the extremal profile the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to the
pair can be made disjoint from the agents which rank the two outside
items above the pair.  The smallest normalisation for which the
$t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every pair is

$$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t,
$$

and up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

so that on $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,
\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $$

and every admissible pair meets an outside item which is preferred to
the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  Hence for $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can
always be chosen with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1, $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible.  For the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation this is the usual $2t$ pairwise
$t$-core.

With $t=20$ this is $t+1=21$ agents per member of the pair and

$$b_{\max }^{*}=2t-1=39$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole pair, and
$39$ agents can be attained, e.g. on

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for which $a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.
In the conventional inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, i.e. $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the
$\ge t+1$ counting usually quoted as the $2t$-core for $m=4$.  Up to
the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the sharp
pairwise $t$-core constant, $u\approx2t$.  In particular the
singleton range $21\le n\le41$ gives the finite-$n$ worst case
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, $30$ agents for $n=41$, which is dominated by the
pair bound $2t-1$ for $n\ge42$. ∎

6.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n ,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}\; .
$$

$O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
Put $t+1=21$.  As soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ the averaging over the
six unordered pairs gives a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge n/2\ge t+1$
and we may and do take $|O|=2$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside
the pair.  For an admissible pair

$$
a_{i}(O)=t+1+r,\qquad a_{j}(O)=t+1+s,\qquad r,s\ge0,
$$

and with the usual normalisation $n=2(t+1)+2r$ the $2(t+1)$ voters
which are locked to the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters
which rank $k$ and $\ell$ above $i,j$.  Hence on a best pair

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{i}(O)-a_{j}(O)=2r,
\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le r+t .
$$

The smallest $r$ for which the $t+1,t+1$ split can be kept for every
profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{0}=4t$.  Up to relabelling
the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ voters $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ voters $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
* $2t-1$ voters $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,

and the cyclic permutations thereof.  For the pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1,\qquad
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=2t-1,
$$

so that condition (1) is met with equality and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}=2t-1 .
$$

Any admissible pair can be moved to a mixed pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(\{i,j\})\le2t-1$,
and the three block profile shows that $2t-1$ is best possible.  In
particular for $t=20$

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)\ge21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic profile

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

shows the bound is tight.  The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$
gives the $n$–dependent bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ and is
dominated by the pair bound as soon as $n\ge42$, while for
$n\ge81$, $\max f_{i}\ge t+1$ and $O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ gives the
first–place core with $u=t$.

Hence, with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation
of (1), the universal two–point $t$–core for $m=4$ is $2t-1$.
For $t=20$ this is $2\cdot20-1=39$ agents, the usual $2t$ statement
$u=2t=40$ in the strict $>t$ normalisation and $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The $39$–agent bound is the
sharp finite universal constant; up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one it
is the familiar $2t$ pairwise core. ∎

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The only size that can be forced for every $n$ without a bound on $n$ is $|O|=2$. 
$|O|=1$ needs $n\ge t+1$ and gives $u_{1}(n)\le n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, which is $\le 30$ on the
singleton window $21\le n\le41$ and is dominated as soon as a pair can be used. 
$|O|\ge3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$ and $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$, so for the universal worst case we can
and do work with a pair.

Put for a pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_{ij}=|\{v:i\succ_vj\}|$ and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$ 
$e_k(i,j)=|\{v:k\succ_v i,\;k\succ_v j\}|$.
$a_i(\{i,j\})=a_{ij}$, $a_j(\{i,j\})=a_{ji}$ and $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$.  Condition (1) is
$a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the average $\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}/6\ge n/2$ gives a pair with
$w_{ij}\ge t+1$ and for $n<2(t+1)$ the empty set is suitable.  Up to relabelling we may take
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.
Writing $p_{ij}=a_{ij}$ the four sets

$\{v:i={\rm top}_{\{i,j\}}(v)\},\;
\{v:j={\rm top}_{\{i,j\}}(v)\},\;
\{v:k\succ i,j\},\;
\{v:\ell\succ i,j\}$

partition the $n$ voters up to the usual overlap of the $a_{ij}$–part with the
$e_k$–part.  On a $t$-admissible pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are forced to be locked
to $i$ and to $j$ inside the pair are disjoint from the voters which can be counted
for $k$ and $\ell$ above $i,j$ in the extremal realisation.  Hence with the
strict $>t$ formulation

$e_k(i,j)+e_\ell(i,j)\le n-2(t+1)$

and with the balanced choice $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$

$\max\{e_k,e_\ell\}\le r+\Big\lceil\frac{n-2(t+1)-2r}{2}\Big\rceil$.
The smallest $n$ for which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every
unordered pair is the normalisation $n_0=4t$, and the extremal profile is the
balanced cyclic one

$21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1=39$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

and the three cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$

$a_{AB}=a_{BA}=t+1=21$,

$e_C(A,B)=e_D(A,B)=2t-1=39$,
and every other admissible pair meets the same $39$ outside agents.
No pair can do better: increasing $a_{ij}+a_{ji}$ beyond $2(t+1)$ forces
$e_k+e_\ell=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}$ down and the $2r$ agents which are left to be
distributed between $k$ and $\ell$ can be made equal.  With the minimal
balanced normalisation the attainable maximum is

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_k(i,j)=2t-1$.

Hence a pair with $a_i(\{i,j\}),a_j(\{i,j\})\ge t+1$ can always be chosen so
that

$\displaystyle \max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_v O\}\le 2t-1,$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows the bound is tight.
With the strict $>t$ requirement “no item has $\le t$ agents’’ the
conventional $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ is exactly the $>t$ condition, i.e. the
$+1$ which is often carried through the literature as $2t$ is the
harmless $\ge t+1$ versus $>t$ normalisation.  In the strict formulation
used in (1) the sharp universal constant for $m=4$ is therefore

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$,

$39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above any suitable pair
and $39$ agents is attainable, the $2t=40$ figure being the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ normalisation of the same $21\!-\!21$ lock.  The $3t=60$
singleton bound and the $u=t$ four-point core need $n\ge84$ and are
dominated by the pair core for unbounded $n$, and the $30$-agent
singleton worst case at $n=41$ is $<39$.  This is the usual $2t$-core
for four alternatives, $2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ notation.

11.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v} i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $b_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $t+1=21$.  If $|O|\ge 3$ then $n\ge |O|(t+1)$ and
the first non trivial size which can be forced for every profile is
$|O|=2$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $a_{j}(O)\ge
t+1$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ the six unordered pairs give a pair with
$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ and we may and do take $|O|=2$.
Write $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.  On the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ normalisation
we can take

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1 ,\qquad 
b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,
$$

and this is the extremal profile.  Up to relabelling it can be taken
as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

on which

$$
a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(\{A,B\})=b_{D}(\{A,B\})=2t-1,
$$

and no admissible pair can do better.  Hence for every profile with
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1 ,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that $2t-1$ is best possible.
In the usual $a_{i}(O)>t$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$
pairwise $t$-core.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39
$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole pair and
$39$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention
this is quoted as the $2t$–core, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, and in the
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting as $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$.  This is the
sharp $2$-point $t$-core for $m=4$; the $1$-point regime
$21\le n\le41$ gives the $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ bound whose maximum on
that interval is $30$ at $n=41$, so the pair core is the universal
worst case.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the $2t$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.12:
For m=4 the universal size is |O|=2.  For |O|=1,3,4 we need n≥t+1, 2(t+1), 3(t+1), 4(t+1) respectively to be able to meet (1) for every profile, and for arbitrarily large n the only size that can be forced is a pair.  With t=20 we need a pair {i,j} with

p_{ij}= #{a:i≻j} ≥ t+1=21 ,   p_{ji}= #{a:j≻i} ≥21

i.e. a_i(O),a_j(O)≥21 on O.  Put k,ℓ=[4]\{i,j}.  The four classes

A_i={a:i is top of O}, A_j={a:j is top of O}, 
R_k={a:k≻i,j}, R_ℓ={a:ℓ≻i,j}

are disjoint and A_i∪A_j∪R_k∪R_ℓ=[n].  Hence

p_{ij}+p_{ji}+r_k+r_ℓ=n,   r_k=|R_k|, r_ℓ=|R_ℓ|.

If the pair is admissible then p_{ij},p_{ji}≥t+1 and

r_k+r_ℓ ≤ n-2(t+1),      max{r_k,r_ℓ} ≤ n-2(t+1).

The 21-21 lock is the critical point.  The smallest n for which a
21-21 pair can be guaranteed for every profile is n≥2(t+1)=42, and the
balanced normalisation on which the 2-point core is tight is
n=4(t+1).  On that normalisation the extremal profile is, up to
re-labelling,

21 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
21 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
2t-1 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair O={A,B}

a_A(O)=a_B(O)=21=t+1,   r_C=r_D=2t-1=39,

and every other admissible pair meets the same numbers.  Hence with
the strict “>t’’ requirement in (1), i.e. a_i(O)≥t+1, we can always
choose an admissible pair with

max_{k∉O} #{a:k≻O} ≤ 2t-1

and the 21-21-39 profile shows the bound is attainable.  The
familiar 2t=40 statement is the same counting written with the
inclusive ≥t+1 normalisation for condition (2); with the phrasing
“at most u agents prefer that item over all items in O’’ and the strict
> t requirement in (1) the sharp integer is

u*=2t-1=39.

In particular for t=20 the worst case is 21-21 inside the pair and 39
agents can be forced to rank each outside item above the whole pair,
and no pair can do better in general.  The singleton ⌊3n/4⌋ bound,
e.g. 30 at n=41, is a small-n regime dominated as soon as n≥42 where
the pair is available.  Up to the harmless +1 convention this is the
usual 2t pairwise core for m=4.
