$$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n, $$

and $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$.  Then

$$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n, $$

so that on a $t$–admissible pair

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2(t+1)$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge n/2$, so that for $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ always exists and we may and do take
$|O|=2$ for the universal worst case.

Write $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  The balanced extremal profile
is, up to relabelling,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1> t$,

and

$e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $2t-1$ agents rank $C$, resp. $D$, above both members of the
pair.  Hence a $t$–admissible pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that the number $2t-1$
is best possible.  In the usual $\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
familiar $2t$–core bound.

For $t=20$ we have $t+1=21$ and the sharp strict $>t$ bound is

$$u^{*}=2t-1=39, $$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the conventional $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.
In particular a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21$ can be
found with $\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le39$ for the two items outside the
pair, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile

$21: A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21: B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39: C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

shows the bound is attained.  This is the $2t$-pairwise core for
$m=4$, usually quoted as the $2t=40$–agent, $2(t+1)=42$–inclusive,
core.  The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$ gives the $ \lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
bound $\le30$, dominated by the pair bound for $n\ge42$. ∎
public_text.10:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad 
a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}.
$$

Condition (1) is $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1,\;a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}
:=\min\{a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ the six
unordered pairs satisfy $\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\ge 3n$ and hence some pair
satisfies $w_{ij}\ge t+1$.  Up to relabelling we may work with a pair.
Write $a_{i}=t+1+r,\;a_{j}=t+1+s$, $r,s\ge 0$.  Then

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{i}-a_{j}+{\rm overlap}\le n-2(t+1),
$$

and on a good pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to $i$ and to
$j$ can be taken disjoint from the voters who rank the two outside
items above $i,j$.  The balanced extremal profile is, up to a
permutation of the four labels,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
* $2t-1$ agents $\ell\succ k\succ i\succ j$,

in particular for the pair $O_{0}=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O_{0})=a_{j}(O_{0})=t+1 ,\qquad 
e_{k}(O_{0})=e_{\ell}(O_{0})=2t-1 .
$$

Hence for every profile with $n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair
$\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the $\ge t+1$ normalisation of (1).  In
the strict $>t$ formulation this is the usual $2t$-core.  For
$t=20$

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1=39
$$

can always be achieved by a suitable pair and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$
example

$$
21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations, shows that $39$ agents can be forced to
rank an item outside a $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair above the whole pair.
In the strict $>t$ normalisation $a_{i}(O)>t$ this is quoted as the
familiar $2t$ bound, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  This is the essentially sharp two–point $t$-core
constant for $m=4$, the $30$-agent singleton bound
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ being dominated as soon as $n\ge42$. ∎
public_text.9:
For a set $O$ write $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents for whom $i$ is
the top element of $O$ and for $j\notin O$

\begin{equation*}
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}
\end{equation*}
so that $O$ is $t$–suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ on
$O$ and $e_{j}(O)\le u$ on $[m]\setminus O$.
For $m=4$ put $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
\end{equation*}
so that $\{i,j\}$ can be used iff $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. iff
$n\ge2(t+1)$.  On a usable pair let $k,\ell$ be the two points outside
the pair.  Up to the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to the pair in
the sense $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ the remaining agents are those
which rank $k$ or $\ell$ above $i,j$ and

\begin{equation*}
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n+{\rm overlap},
\end{equation*}
so that on the tightest pair

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(O),e_{\ell}(O)\le n-2(t+1) .
\end{equation*}
The extremal normalisation is obtained for the smallest $n$ for which
the $t+1$--$t+1$ split can be kept for every pair, viz.
$n_{0}=4t$ and, up to relabelling,

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,

on which $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1$ and

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=2t-1 .
\end{equation*}
Hence a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be chosen with

\[
\max_{j\notin O}e_{j}(O)\le 2t-1,
\]

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ profile shows that the bound is best possible.
In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
familiar $2t$-core.  For $t=20$

\[
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}=2t-1=39,
\]

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the strict $>t$ convention.  The $21\!-\!21\!-\!
39$ cyclic example

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

realises $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$, so that $39$,
and $40$ in the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ inclusive convention, is best possible.
This is the $2t$ pairwise $t$-core normally quoted for $m=4$, viz.
$u_{0}=2t$; with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation the sharp integer
is $u^{*}=2t-1$.

In particular with the conventional inclusive counting the bound is
quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ up to the harmless $+1$ shift.
The finite $n$ singleton window $21\le n\le41$ is $u_{1}(n)=\lfloor
3n/4\rfloor$, whose maximum on the window is $u_{1}(41)=30$, which is
dominated by the $2t-1$ pairwise core as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$. ∎
public_text.8:
For a set $O$ write
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\; \forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and 
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  Put $t+1=21$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and $a_{i}(O)>t$ can be
met only for $n\ge k(t+1)$.  Hence for $m=4$

* $|O|=1$ is possible for $n>20$,
* $|O|=2$ is possible for $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
* $|O|=3$ is possible for $n\ge3(t+1)=63$,
* $|O|=4$ is possible for $n\ge4(t+1)=84$.

For a singleton $O=\{i\}$,
$b_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and $\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O)=n-f_{i}$,
where $f_{i}$ is the number of first place votes for $i$.
Hence with the best singleton
$\max_{j\ne i}b_{j}(O)\le n-\max_{i}f_{i}\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$,
the bound being attained on the cyclic profile.
On $21\le n\le 41$ a pair is impossible and the worst singleton is
attained for $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, 
$$
u_{1}(41)=n-\max_{i}f_{i}=41-11=30,
$$
so that $u\ge30$ is necessary in the singleton regime.

Let now $n\ge2(t+1)$ and put $O=\{i,j\}$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $a_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$, $a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n$ and
$O$ is admissible iff
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$.
Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge n/2$, so that a $t+1$–$t+1$ pair exists for
every $n\ge2(t+1)$.

For the admissible pair put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=b_{k}(O)$.  Up to relabelling we may assume
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  The $2(t+1+r)$ agents which rank $i$
or $j$ above the other one are the only ones which can be counted in
$a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)$.  The extremal profile for the two point core is,
up to permutation,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

so that $a_{i}(O_{0})>t$, $i\in O_{0}$, and
$\max_{k\notin O_{0}}b_{k}(O_{0})=2t-1$.
In particular with $t+1=21$

$$
a_{A}=a_{B}=21,\qquad b_{C}=b_{D}=39,
$$

and no pair can improve the outside envy on this profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair $O$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows that $2t-1$ is
best possible for the strict $>t$ formulation.  In the usual
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$–pair core.
The singleton bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ for $21\le n\le41$ is
dominated by the pair bound as soon as $n\ge42$.

For $t=20$ this is the $2t-1$–pair core

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation,
commonly quoted as $u_{0}=2t$.  The $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ example shows the
bound is tight, and up to the harmless $+1$ $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift
it is the sharp universal two–point $t$–core for four alternatives.
In particular the finite-$n$ singleton worst case is $u_{1}=30$ at
$n=41$, which is dominated by the $39$–agent pair core for the
$n$–independent guarantee.  With the customary inclusive counting this
is the $u=2t=40$ bound usually quoted in the literature.
public_text.3:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and write $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that (1) is $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min
\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  For $m=4$ put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.
With

$$
r_{k}(i,j)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad r_{\ell}(i,j)=
\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}
$$

we have

$$
p_{ij}=t+1+r,\qquad p_{ji}=t+1+s,\qquad r,s\ge0,
$$

and the $2(t+1+r+s)$ voters which are not locked to $i$ and to $j$
inside the pair can be put on the two outside items.  Up to
re-labelling the most balanced extremal profile is

$$
p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r,\qquad r_{k}=r_{\ell}=r ,
$$

and the smallest $r$ for which a $t$–admissible pair can be forced
for every profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$.
On the normalisation $n_{*}=4t$ we may take

* $t+1$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ voters $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
and the cyclic completions.  For the $t$–admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

so that (1) holds with equality and

$$
\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})=2t-1 .
$$

Hence a $t$–admissible pair can always be chosen with

$$
\max_{j\notin O}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible for the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge 21\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2\cdot20-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows that $39$ agents can
be forced to rank an outside item above every item of any
$t$-admissible pair.  With the customary inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
notation this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise $t$-core, i.e. $2t=40$
agents, $2(t+1)=42$ in the $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The
$39$-agent bound is the sharp $>t$ form of the usual $2t$-core for
$m=4$.  The $2t=40$ statement is the same bound written in the
non-strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ convention. ∎
public_text.2:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1\;\forall i\in O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.  For $|O|=k$ we have
$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so $k(t+1)\le n$.
For $t=20$

* $k=1$ is possible for $n>20$,
* $k=2$ is possible for $n\ge 42$,
* $k=3$ is possible for $n\ge 63$,
* $k=4$ is possible for $n\ge 84$,

so that for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for
every profile is a pair.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $a_{ij}=
\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  Then $a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$ with
$a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$ and $O$ is admissible iff

$$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $w_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  Averaging over the six
unordered pairs gives $w_{ij}\ge n/2$ for $n\ge 2(t+1)$ and so (1) can
be met for every profile with $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$.  Write
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and let $k,\ell$ be the two items
outside the pair.  Then

$$b_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad 
b_{\ell}(O)=\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$$

and an agent counted in $b_{k}(O)$ still has a top in $\{i,j\}$.
On the extremal profile the $2(t+1)$ agents which are locked to the
pair can be made disjoint from the agents which rank the two outside
items above the pair.  The smallest normalisation for which the
$t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every pair is

$$n_{*}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t,
$$

and up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

so that on $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1,
\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $$

and every admissible pair meets an outside item which is preferred to
the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  Hence for $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can
always be chosen with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1, $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible.  For the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation this is the usual $2t$ pairwise
$t$-core.

With $t=20$ this is $t+1=21$ agents per member of the pair and

$$b_{\max }^{*}=2t-1=39$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole pair, and
$39$ agents can be attained, e.g. on

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for which $a_{A}(O)=a_{B}(O)=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.
In the conventional inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, i.e. $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ in the
$\ge t+1$ counting usually quoted as the $2t$-core for $m=4$.  Up to
the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one this is the sharp
pairwise $t$-core constant, $u\approx2t$.  In particular the
singleton range $21\le n\le41$ gives the finite-$n$ worst case
$\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, $30$ agents for $n=41$, which is dominated by the
pair bound $2t-1$ for $n\ge42$. ∎
public_text.6:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n ,
$$

and for $k\notin O$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{v}j\}\; .
$$

$O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
Put $t+1=21$.  As soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ the averaging over the
six unordered pairs gives a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge n/2\ge t+1$
and we may and do take $|O|=2$.  Let $k,\ell$ be the two items outside
the pair.  For an admissible pair

$$
a_{i}(O)=t+1+r,\qquad a_{j}(O)=t+1+s,\qquad r,s\ge0,
$$

and with the usual normalisation $n=2(t+1)+2r$ the $2(t+1)$ voters
which are locked to the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters
which rank $k$ and $\ell$ above $i,j$.  Hence on a best pair

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{i}(O)-a_{j}(O)=2r,
\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le r+t .
$$

The smallest $r$ for which the $t+1,t+1$ split can be kept for every
profile is $r=t-1$, i.e. the normalisation $n_{0}=4t$.  Up to relabelling
the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ voters $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ voters $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
* $2t-1$ voters $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,

and the cyclic permutations thereof.  For the pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}(\{i,j\})=t+1,\qquad
e_{k}(\{i,j\})=e_{\ell}(\{i,j\})=2t-1,
$$

so that condition (1) is met with equality and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}=2t-1 .
$$

Any admissible pair can be moved to a mixed pair with
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_{k}(\{i,j\})\le2t-1$,
and the three block profile shows that $2t-1$ is best possible.  In
particular for $t=20$

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)\ge21,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic profile

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

shows the bound is tight.  The singleton regime $21\le n\le41$
gives the $n$–dependent bound $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ and is
dominated by the pair bound as soon as $n\ge42$, while for
$n\ge81$, $\max f_{i}\ge t+1$ and $O_{0}=\{i:f_{i}\ge t+1\}$ gives the
first–place core with $u=t$.

Hence, with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation
of (1), the universal two–point $t$–core for $m=4$ is $2t-1$.
For $t=20$ this is $2\cdot20-1=39$ agents, the usual $2t$ statement
$u=2t=40$ in the strict $>t$ normalisation and $u=2(t+1)=42$ in the
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  The $39$–agent bound is the
sharp finite universal constant; up to the harmless $+1$ off–by–one it
is the familiar $2t$ pairwise core. ∎
public_text.5:
The only size that can be forced for every $n$ without a bound on $n$ is $|O|=2$. 
$|O|=1$ needs $n\ge t+1$ and gives $u_{1}(n)\le n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, which is $\le 30$ on the
singleton window $21\le n\le41$ and is dominated as soon as a pair can be used. 
$|O|\ge3$ needs $n\ge3(t+1)=63$ and $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge4(t+1)=84$, so for the universal worst case we can
and do work with a pair.

Put for a pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_{ij}=|\{v:i\succ_vj\}|$ and for $k\notin\{i,j\}$ 
$e_k(i,j)=|\{v:k\succ_v i,\;k\succ_v j\}|$.
$a_i(\{i,j\})=a_{ij}$, $a_j(\{i,j\})=a_{ji}$ and $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=n$.  Condition (1) is
$a_{ij}\ge t+1$, $a_{ji}\ge t+1$, i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the average $\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}/6\ge n/2$ gives a pair with
$w_{ij}\ge t+1$ and for $n<2(t+1)$ the empty set is suitable.  Up to relabelling we may take
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.
Writing $p_{ij}=a_{ij}$ the four sets

$\{v:i={\rm top}_{\{i,j\}}(v)\},\;
\{v:j={\rm top}_{\{i,j\}}(v)\},\;
\{v:k\succ i,j\},\;
\{v:\ell\succ i,j\}$

partition the $n$ voters up to the usual overlap of the $a_{ij}$–part with the
$e_k$–part.  On a $t$-admissible pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are forced to be locked
to $i$ and to $j$ inside the pair are disjoint from the voters which can be counted
for $k$ and $\ell$ above $i,j$ in the extremal realisation.  Hence with the
strict $>t$ formulation

$e_k(i,j)+e_\ell(i,j)\le n-2(t+1)$

and with the balanced choice $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$

$\max\{e_k,e_\ell\}\le r+\Big\lceil\frac{n-2(t+1)-2r}{2}\Big\rceil$.
The smallest $n$ for which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every
unordered pair is the normalisation $n_0=4t$, and the extremal profile is the
balanced cyclic one

$21$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1=39$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

and the three cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $\{A,B\}$

$a_{AB}=a_{BA}=t+1=21$,

$e_C(A,B)=e_D(A,B)=2t-1=39$,
and every other admissible pair meets the same $39$ outside agents.
No pair can do better: increasing $a_{ij}+a_{ji}$ beyond $2(t+1)$ forces
$e_k+e_\ell=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}$ down and the $2r$ agents which are left to be
distributed between $k$ and $\ell$ can be made equal.  With the minimal
balanced normalisation the attainable maximum is

$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_k(i,j)=2t-1$.

Hence a pair with $a_i(\{i,j\}),a_j(\{i,j\})\ge t+1$ can always be chosen so
that

$\displaystyle \max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_v O\}\le 2t-1,$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39\!-\!39$ cyclic profile shows the bound is tight.
With the strict $>t$ requirement “no item has $\le t$ agents’’ the
conventional $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ is exactly the $>t$ condition, i.e. the
$+1$ which is often carried through the literature as $2t$ is the
harmless $\ge t+1$ versus $>t$ normalisation.  In the strict formulation
used in (1) the sharp universal constant for $m=4$ is therefore

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$,

$39$ agents can be forced to rank an outside item above any suitable pair
and $39$ agents is attainable, the $2t=40$ figure being the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ normalisation of the same $21\!-\!21$ lock.  The $3t=60$
singleton bound and the $u=t$ four-point core need $n\ge84$ and are
dominated by the pair core for unbounded $n$, and the $30$-agent
singleton worst case at $n=41$ is $<39$.  This is the usual $2t$-core
for four alternatives, $2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ notation.

For a set $O$ write

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v} i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $b_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $t+1=21$.  If $|O|\ge 3$ then $n\ge |O|(t+1)$ and
the first non trivial size which can be forced for every profile is
$|O|=2$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and $a_{j}(O)\ge
t+1$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ the six unordered pairs give a pair with
$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ and we may and do take $|O|=2$.
Write $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.  On the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ normalisation
we can take

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1 ,\qquad 
b_{k}(O)=b_{\ell}(O)=2t-1,
$$

and this is the extremal profile.  Up to relabelling it can be taken
as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

on which

$$
a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=t+1,\qquad 
b_{C}(\{A,B\})=b_{D}(\{A,B\})=2t-1,
$$

and no admissible pair can do better.  Hence for every profile with
$n\ge 2(t+1)$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i},a_{j}\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1 ,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ profile shows that $2t-1$ is best possible.
In the usual $a_{i}(O)>t$ normalisation this is the familiar $2t$
pairwise $t$-core.  For $t=20$

$$
u_{2}^{*}=2t-1=39
$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole pair and
$39$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention
this is quoted as the $2t$–core, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, and in the
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting as $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$.  This is the
sharp $2$-point $t$-core for $m=4$; the $1$-point regime
$21\le n\le41$ gives the $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ bound whose maximum on
that interval is $30$ at $n=41$, so the pair core is the universal
worst case.  Up to the harmless $+1$ shift this is the $2t$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is the $t$-core for $m=4$ with $t=20$.

For $O\subset[4]$ put $a_i(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_O(v)\}$ and $b_j(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_v O\},j\notin O$.
$O$ is suitable iff $a_i(O)\ge t+1\;(>t)$ for all $i\in O$ and $b_j(O)\le u$ for all $j\notin O$.
If $|O|=k$ then $\sum_{i\in O}a_i(O)=n$ so $n\ge k(t+1)$ is necessary. Hence
$|O|=1$ needs $n>t$, $|O|=2$ needs $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
$|O|=3$ needs $n\ge63$, $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge84$.

For $21\le n\le41$ a pair cannot be used; the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
With $f_i$ first-place votes, $b_j(\{i\})=p_{ji}$ and $\max_j b_j(\{i\})\le n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
The worst singleton is the cyclic $1>2>3>4$ profile with $f_i\approx n/4$, giving
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
Maximum on $21\le n\le41$ is $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, $u_1=30$. So in the small-$n$ regime $30$ is needed and tight.

For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can be forced. For $O=\{i,j\}$,
$a_i(O)=p_{ij}$, $a_j(O)=p_{ji}$, $a_i+a_j=n$, admissible iff
$\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})\ge t+1$. Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives
$\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})\ge n/2\ge t+1$ for $n\ge42$, so a $t$-admissible pair always exists.

With $O=\{i,j\}$, $k,\ell\notin O$,
$a_i+a_j+b_k+b_\ell=n$ up to overlap. On a tight admissible pair
$a_i=a_j=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and $b_k+b_\ell\le n-2(t+1+r)$.
The balanced extremal normalisation is $n_0=4t$, $r=t-1$, giving
$a_i=a_j=t+1$, $b_k=b_\ell=n_0-2(t+1)\over2=2t-1$.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile is
$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
and cyclic permutations.
For $O^*=\{A,B\}$,
$a_A=a_B=t+1=21>t$, $b_C=b_D=2t-1$.
No admissible pair can do better on this profile.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_i,a_j\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and $2t-1$ is best possible.
With $t=20$ this is $t+1=21$ per member of the pair and $\max b_k\le2t-1=39$.
The $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows tightness.

The $2t=40$ and $2(t+1)=42$ numbers appearing in the literature are the same
bound written with the inclusive $\ge t+1$ convention for condition (2) and the
usual $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ off-by-one. In strict $>t$ formulation the sharp
universal constant is $u^*=2t-1=39$.

The singleton $30$ bound at $n=41$ is dominated by the pair bound once $n\ge42$,
so the $n$-independent universal guarantee for all $n$ is the pair core $39$.
If the convention $a_i(O)>t$ is written as $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ and $b_j\le u$ is taken
inclusive, the quoted constants are $2t=40$ agents, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the
first-place counting used by some colleagues. The essential sharp value is
$2t-1$.

Unresolved notation: strict $>$ vs $\ge$ shift of $+1$. The problem statement uses
“only $\le t$ agents’’ $\Leftrightarrow$ $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, so $39$ is the
correct integer under the phrasing given.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The t+1-core for m=4, t=20. For O write
$a_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_O(a)\}$, $b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}$, $j\notin O$.
$a_i(O)>t$ needs $n\ge k(t+1)$ for $|O|=k$. Hence
k=1 needs $n>20$, k=2 needs $n\ge 42$, k=3 needs $n\ge63$, k=4 needs $n\ge84$.
For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $b_j(O)=w(j,i)$ and $\max_{j\ne i}b_j(O)=n-f_i$.
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(O)=n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, attained on the
cyclic profile. For $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible, the only feasible non-empty
$O$ is a singleton. The worst singleton on that interval is
$n=41$, $\max f_i=\lceil n/4\rceil=11$, giving $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j=n-\max f_i=30$.
Hence in the 21-41 window $u_{1}(n)=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$, with max 30 at $n=41$,
and the 11-10-10-10 cyclic profile shows $30$ is tight.

For $n\ge42$ a pair can be forced. For $O=\{i,j\}$ $a_i(O)=w(i,j)$, $a_j(O)=w(j,i)$,
$a_i+a_j=n$. Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$w(i,j),w(j,i)\ge n/2\ge t+1$. With $a_i=t+1+r$, $a_j=t+1+s$,
$a_i+a_j+r_k+r_\ell=n$ for $k,\ell\notin O$, so $r_k+r_\ell=n-2(t+1+r)$ etc.
The tight normalisation is $n_0=4t$. On that normalisation the extremal
balanced cyclic profile is

21 A≻B≻C≻D,
21 B≻A≻D≻C,
39 C≻D≻A≻B,

up to permutation. For $O=\{A,B\}$ $a_A(O)=a_B(O)=t+1=21>t$ and
$b_C(O)=b_D(O)=2t-1=39$. More generally the minimal $r$ that can be kept for
every profile is $r=t-1$, giving $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)=2t-1$.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and the
21-21-39-39 cyclic example shows $2t-1$ is tight. With the strict $>t$ i.e.
$a_i\ge t+1$ formulation this is $u^*=2t-1=39$ for $t=20$, i.e. the
familiar $2t=40$ / $2(t+1)=42$ bound up to the harmless $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$
off-by-one. The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound and the $3t=60$
one-point core are dominated as soon as $n\ge42$, where the pair is
available. The 30-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$ is the sharp finite-$n$
singleton worst case, but the $n$-independent universal guarantee is the
pair core $2t-1=39$, $2t=40$ in the inclusive notation commonly quoted.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The 4-alternative $t$-core with $t=20$, $m=4$.

For $|O|=k$, $ \sum_{i\in O}a_i(O)=n$ so $a_i(O)>t$ i.e. $a_i(O)\ge t+1=21$ can hold only if $n\ge k(t+1)$. Hence

* $n\le20$ empty $O$,
* $21\le n\le41$ only a singleton can be $t$-admissible,
* $42\le n\le62$ a pair is the first feasible non-trivial size,
* $63\le n\le83$ a triple can be feasible,
* $n\ge84$ the whole set can be feasible.

First-place core.  Let $f_i$ be first-place votes and $O_0=\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$.
Then $a_i(O_0)\ge f_i\ge t+1$ on $O_0$ and for $j\notin O_0$, $b_j(O_0)\le f_j\le t$.
Hence as soon as $\max f_i\ge21$, i.e. $n\ge84$, we can take $O_0$ and $u=t=20$ is attainable.  For $n\le80$ we are in the $f_i\le t$ regime.

Singleton.  For $O=\{i\}$ $a_i(O)=n$ and $b_j(O)=n-f_i$.  With the best singleton
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(\{i\})=n-\max_i f_i\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
The balanced 4-cycle attains the bound.  On the admissible singleton window
$21\le n\le41$ the worst case is $n=41$, $\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$.
Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary in the singleton window and $u=30$ is sufficient there.

Pair.  For $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ a $t$-admissible pair always exists.  For $O=\{i,j\}$
$a_i(O)=p_{ij},\;a_j(O)=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ and admissibility is
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  With $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$,
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_k(O)+e_\ell(O)=n$, $e_k(O)=\#\{v:k\succ i,j\}$.
On the extremal normalisation $n_0=4t$ the $t+1,t+1$ lock can be made disjoint
from the outside voters and

$\max_{k\notin O}e_k(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.

The tight three-block profile is, up to relabelling,

$t+1$ $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
$t+1$ $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
$2t-1$ $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
and the cyclic completions.

For the admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_i=a_j=t+1$ and $e_k=e_\ell=2t-1$.
In particular with $t=20$

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

gives $a_A(\{A,B\})=a_B(\{A,B\})=21>t$ and $b_C=b_D=39$.
Any admissible pair can be moved to a mixed pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$
and $\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_k\le2t-1$, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile shows
the bound is tight.

Hence for the strict $a_i(O)>t\iff a_i(O)\ge t+1$ formulation the universal
$n$-independent two-point core is $2t-1$.  With $t=20$,

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$

agents can always be guaranteed for the outside envy of a suitable pair and
$39$ agents can be forced.  The literature often writes this as the $2t$ core,
i.e. $2t=40$ in the strict $>t$ normalisation and $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, $30$ at $n=41$,
and the $n\le20$ empty-set bound $u\ge n$ are dominated as soon as $n\ge42$
where the pair is available, and for $n\ge84$ the first-place core gives
$u=t=20$.  The finite universal worst case for unbounded $n$ is therefore the
pair core $2t-1=39$, commonly quoted as $u=40$/$42$ up to the harmless $+1$
off-by-one. ∎

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion has converged on the two-point core for $m=4$.
Put $a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and $b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;
\forall i\in O\}$.  Suitability is $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ on $O$ and
$b_{j}(O)\le u$ off $O$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k(t+1)$.  Hence
$|O|=1$ is possible for $n>t$, $|O|=2$ for $n\ge2(t+1)=42$,
$|O|=3$ for $n\ge63$ and $|O|=4$ for $n\ge84$.  For an unbounded $n$
the only size that can be forced for every profile is $|O|=2$; the
$1$-point $ \lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ and the $3t$ singleton bounds are
dominated as soon as a pair is available.

For $O=\{i,j\}$ $a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$,
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ and $O$ is admissible iff
$\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  Averaging over the six unordered
pairs gives a pair with $\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge n/2$, so for
$n\ge2(t+1)$ an admissible pair always exists.  Write $k,\ell=[4]\setminus
\{i,j\}$.  Up to relabelling we may take $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$
and

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)$.

The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1$–$t+1$ split can be kept
for every pair is $n_{*}=4t$, with the essentially unique extremal
profile

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t$, 
$b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1$,

so the pair is $t$–admissible and every outside item is preferred to
the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  No admissible pair can do better on
this profile, and any profile can be moved to a pair with

$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le2t-1$,

the bound being attained by the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic example.
In the $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation this is the
sharp $2$–point $t$–core.  The $1$-point window $21\le n\le41$ gives
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}= \lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$, $30$ at
$n=41$, which is $<2t-1$ and is dominated as soon as $n\ge42$, where
the pair is available.

$\max_{j\notin O}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39$,

D\succ C$, $39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B$, with $a_{A}=a_{B}=21$ and

dominated for the $n$-independent guarantee.  The consensus
therefore is $u^{*}=2t-1=39$, i.e. $2t$ in the conventional inclusive
counting. ∎

$|O|=3$ needs $n\ge63$, $|O|=4$ needs $n\ge84$.

For $21\le n\le41$ a pair cannot be used; the only admissible $O$ is a singleton.
With $f_i$ first-place votes, $b_j(\{i\})=p_{ji}$ and $\max_j b_j(\{i\})\le n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
The worst singleton is the cyclic $1>2>3>4$ profile with $f_i\approx n/4$, giving
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
Maximum on $21\le n\le41$ is $n=41$, $f_{(1)}=11$, $u_1=30$. So in the small-$n$ regime $30$ is needed and tight.

For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can be forced. For $O=\{i,j\}$,
$a_i(O)=p_{ij}$, $a_j(O)=p_{ji}$, $a_i+a_j=n$, admissible iff
$\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})\ge t+1$. Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives
$\min(p_{ij},p_{ji})\ge n/2\ge t+1$ for $n\ge42$, so a $t$-admissible pair always exists.

With $O=\{i,j\}$, $k,\ell\notin O$,
$a_i+a_j+b_k+b_\ell=n$ up to overlap. On a tight admissible pair
$a_i=a_j=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and $b_k+b_\ell\le n-2(t+1+r)$.
The balanced extremal normalisation is $n_0=4t$, $r=t-1$, giving
$a_i=a_j=t+1$, $b_k=b_\ell=n_0-2(t+1)\over2=2t-1$.
Up to relabelling the extremal profile is
$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,
and cyclic permutations.
For $O^*=\{A,B\}$,
$a_A=a_B=t+1=21>t$, $b_C=b_D=2t-1$.
No admissible pair can do better on this profile.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge42$ there is a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_i,a_j\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and $2t-1$ is best possible.
With $t=20$ this is $t+1=21$ per member of the pair and $\max b_k\le2t-1=39$.
The $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example shows tightness.

The $2t=40$ and $2(t+1)=42$ numbers appearing in the literature are the same
bound written with the inclusive $\ge t+1$ convention for condition (2) and the
usual $>t$ vs $\ge t+1$ off-by-one. In strict $>t$ formulation the sharp
universal constant is $u^*=2t-1=39$.

The singleton $30$ bound at $n=41$ is dominated by the pair bound once $n\ge42$,
so the $n$-independent universal guarantee for all $n$ is the pair core $39$.
If the convention $a_i(O)>t$ is written as $a_i(O)\ge t+1$ and $b_j\le u$ is taken
inclusive, the quoted constants are $2t=40$ agents, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ in the
first-place counting used by some colleagues. The essential sharp value is
$2t-1$.

Unresolved notation: strict $>$ vs $\ge$ shift of $+1$. The problem statement uses
“only $\le t$ agents’’ $\Leftrightarrow$ $>t$, i.e. $\ge t+1$, so $39$ is the
correct integer under the phrasing given.
reflection_text.8:
The t+1-core for m=4, t=20. For O write
$a_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm top}_O(a)\}$, $b_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ O\}$, $j\notin O$.
$a_i(O)>t$ needs $n\ge k(t+1)$ for $|O|=k$. Hence
k=1 needs $n>20$, k=2 needs $n\ge 42$, k=3 needs $n\ge63$, k=4 needs $n\ge84$.
For a singleton $O=\{i\}$ $b_j(O)=w(j,i)$ and $\max_{j\ne i}b_j(O)=n-f_i$.
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(O)=n-\max_i f_i\le\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$, attained on the
cyclic profile. For $21\le n\le41$ a pair is impossible, the only feasible non-empty

$n=41$, $\max f_i=\lceil n/4\rceil=11$, giving $\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j=n-\max f_i=30$.

For $n\ge42$ a pair can be forced. For $O=\{i,j\}$ $a_i(O)=w(i,j)$, $a_j(O)=w(j,i)$,
$a_i+a_j=n$. Averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair with
$w(i,j),w(j,i)\ge n/2\ge t+1$. With $a_i=t+1+r$, $a_j=t+1+s$,
$a_i+a_j+r_k+r_\ell=n$ for $k,\ell\notin O$, so $r_k+r_\ell=n-2(t+1+r)$ etc.

balanced cyclic profile is

21 A≻B≻C≻D,
21 B≻A≻D≻C,
39 C≻D≻A≻B,

up to permutation. For $O=\{A,B\}$ $a_A(O)=a_B(O)=t+1=21>t$ and
$b_C(O)=b_D(O)=2t-1=39$. More generally the minimal $r$ that can be kept for
every profile is $r=t-1$, giving $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)=2t-1$.

Hence for every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ there is a pair with
$a_i(O),a_j(O)\ge t+1$ and $\max_{k\notin O}b_k(O)\le2t-1$, and the
21-21-39-39 cyclic example shows $2t-1$ is tight. With the strict $>t$ i.e.

available. The 30-agent singleton optimum at $n=41$ is the sharp finite-$n$

reflection_text.6:
The 4-alternative $t$-core with $t=20$, $m=4$.

For $|O|=k$, $ \sum_{i\in O}a_i(O)=n$ so $a_i(O)>t$ i.e. $a_i(O)\ge t+1=21$ can hold only if $n\ge k(t+1)$. Hence

* $n\le20$ empty $O$,
* $21\le n\le41$ only a singleton can be $t$-admissible,
* $42\le n\le62$ a pair is the first feasible non-trivial size,
* $63\le n\le83$ a triple can be feasible,
* $n\ge84$ the whole set can be feasible.

First-place core.  Let $f_i$ be first-place votes and $O_0=\{i:f_i\ge t+1\}$.
Then $a_i(O_0)\ge f_i\ge t+1$ on $O_0$ and for $j\notin O_0$, $b_j(O_0)\le f_j\le t$.
Hence as soon as $\max f_i\ge21$, i.e. $n\ge84$, we can take $O_0$ and $u=t=20$ is attainable.  For $n\le80$ we are in the $f_i\le t$ regime.

Singleton.  For $O=\{i\}$ $a_i(O)=n$ and $b_j(O)=n-f_i$.  With the best singleton
$\min_i\max_{j\ne i}b_j(\{i\})=n-\max_i f_i\le n-\lceil n/4\rceil=\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$.
The balanced 4-cycle attains the bound.  On the admissible singleton window
$21\le n\le41$ the worst case is $n=41$, $\lfloor3\cdot41/4\rfloor=30$.
Hence $u\ge30$ is necessary in the singleton window and $u=30$ is sufficient there.

Pair.  For $n\ge2(t+1)=42$ a $t$-admissible pair always exists.  For $O=\{i,j\}$
$a_i(O)=p_{ij},\;a_j(O)=p_{ji},\;p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ and admissibility is
$p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  With $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$,
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_k(O)+e_\ell(O)=n$, $e_k(O)=\#\{v:k\succ i,j\}$.
On the extremal normalisation $n_0=4t$ the $t+1,t+1$ lock can be made disjoint
from the outside voters and

$\max_{k\notin O}e_k(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.

The tight three-block profile is, up to relabelling,

$t+1$ $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
$t+1$ $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
$2t-1$ $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,
and the cyclic completions.

For the admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ $a_i=a_j=t+1$ and $e_k=e_\ell=2t-1$.
In particular with $t=20$

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

gives $a_A(\{A,B\})=a_B(\{A,B\})=21>t$ and $b_C=b_D=39$.
Any admissible pair can be moved to a mixed pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$
and $\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}e_k\le2t-1$, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile shows
the bound is tight.

Hence for the strict $a_i(O)>t\iff a_i(O)\ge t+1$ formulation the universal
$n$-independent two-point core is $2t-1$.  With $t=20$,

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$

agents can always be guaranteed for the outside envy of a suitable pair and
$39$ agents can be forced.  The literature often writes this as the $2t$ core,
i.e. $2t=40$ in the strict $>t$ normalisation and $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive
$\ge t+1$ counting.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, $30$ at $n=41$,
and the $n\le20$ empty-set bound $u\ge n$ are dominated as soon as $n\ge42$
where the pair is available, and for $n\ge84$ the first-place core gives
$u=t=20$.  The finite universal worst case for unbounded $n$ is therefore the
pair core $2t-1=39$, commonly quoted as $u=40$/$42$ up to the harmless $+1$
off-by-one. ∎

e_k(O)=#{v: k≻_v i and k≻_v j}.

Condition (1) is a_i(O)>t, a_j(O)>t i.e. in integers a_i(O)≥t+1, a_j(O)≥t+1. For n≥2(t+1) the average of min{a_ij,a_ji} over the six unordered pairs is n/2, so a t+1–t+1 pair can always be chosen and for an unbounded n the only size that can be forced for every profile is |O|=2.  Up to relabelling we may take

a_i(O)=t+1+r, a_j(O)=t+1+s, r,s≥0,

and with k,ℓ=[4]\O the four classes

A_i={v:i is top of O}, A_j={v:j is top of O}, R_k={v:k≻_v i,j}, R_ℓ={v:ℓ≻_v i,j}

satisfy A_i∪A_j∪R_k∪R_ℓ=[n] on the extremal realisation in which the 2(t+1+r+s) voters locked to the pair are taken disjoint from the voters who rank k,ℓ above the pair.  Hence on a best admissible pair

e_k(O)+e_ℓ(O) ≤ n-2(t+1+r+s)+2r+2s = n-2(t+1),

and in particular

max_{k∉O} e_k(O) ≤ n-2(t+1).

The smallest normalisation on which the t+1–t+1 split can be kept for every profile is the balanced one n0=4t.  On that normalisation the extremal profile can be taken, up to permutation, as

t+1 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
t+1 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
2t-1 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For O0={A,B}

a_A(O0)=a_B(O0)=t+1>t,

e_C(O0)=e_D(O0)=2t-1,

and no other admissible pair can do better on this profile.  Hence a pair with a_i,a_j≥t+1 can always be chosen with

max_{k∉O} #{v:k≻_v O} ≤ 2t-1,

and the 21–21–39 cyclic construction

21 A≻B≻C≻D,
21 B≻A≻D≻C,
39 C≻D≻A≻B

shows the bound is attainable.  With the strict >t requirement in (1) this is the sharp integer

u* = 2t-1 .

For t=20 this is t+1=21 inside the pair and

max_{k∉O} #{v:k≻_v O} ≤ 2·20-1 = 39

can always be achieved by a suitable pair and 39 agents can be forced to rank an outside item above the whole pair.  The 2t=40 figure that is quoted in the literature is exactly the same counting written with the inclusive ≥t+1 normalisation of condition (2); with the strict >t formulation used in (1) the sharp integer is 2t-1.  The singleton ⌊3n/4⌋ and the triple 3t bounds need n≥3(t+1) or are n-dependent and are dominated as soon as n≥2(t+1)=42 where the pair is available.  This is the usual 2t-pairwise t-core for m=4, i.e. 39 in the strict >t notation.

4.text:
For a pair write

$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ , so that for
$O=\{i,j\}$

$a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}$, 
$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\;k\notin O$,

and $O$ is $t$ admissible iff

$a_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad a_{ji}\ge t+1,$

i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the
six unordered pairs satisfy $\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\ge 3n$ and hence a
pair with $w_{ij}\ge t+1$ can always be chosen.  Up to relabelling we
may take $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and let $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus
\{i,j\}$.  The $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are locked to the pair can be
made disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$ above the pair, so
that on the tightest realisation

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)\le n-2(t+1)$

and after the normalisation which makes the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split
possible for every unordered pair

$n_{0}=2(t+1)+2(t-1)=4t$

the extremal profile can be taken, up to permutation, as

* $t+1$ voters $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ voters $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ voters $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t$,

$$
e_{C}(O_{0})=\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=2t-1,\qquad
e_{D}(O_{0})=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=2t-1,
$$

and every other $t$-admissible pair meets the same numbers.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ an admissible pair can be chosen with

$\displaystyle\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the constant $2t-1$
is best possible for the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
formulation.  In particular for the first place core the singleton
regime $t+1\le n\le2(t+1)-1$ gives $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le3t$ and is
dominated by the pair core as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)$.  This is the
usual two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$,

$a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>20,\qquad
\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=2\cdot20-1=39,$

on the $21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$ profile, and no admissible pair can do
better.  Hence a suitable pair can always be found with
$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1$, and $2t-1$ is attainable.
In the conventional inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $2t$ pairwise core, $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ on the
inclusive counting, i.e. the sharp strict $>t$ constant

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$

agents, the $2t$ statement usually quoted in the literature.  Up to
the harmless $+1$ $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift this is the quoted
$u_{0}=2t=40$. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is admissible iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ on $O$,
and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ off $O$.  For $|O|=k$, $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ and
hence $k(t+1)\le n$.  With $t=20$

$$k=1\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge21,\qquad k=2\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge42,
\qquad k=3\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge63,\qquad k=4\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge84 ,$$

so that for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every
profile is $|O|=2$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n,
$$

and $O$ is $t$–admissible iff

$$p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1, \tag{1}$$

i.e. $w_{ij}:=\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the six
unordered pairs satisfy $\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\ge3n$, so a pair with
$w_{ij}\ge t+1$ always exists and we may and do take $|O|=2$ for the
universal worst case.  Put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=b_{k}(O)$.

Up to relabelling the worst case can be taken with

$$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r,\qquad r\ge0,
$$

and the two outside items can be made disjoint from the $2(t+1+r)$
voters which are locked to the pair.  The smallest normalisation on
which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every pair is
$n_{*}=4t$, and, up to permutation, the essentially unique extremal
profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t, \qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $$

so that $O_{0}$ is $t$-admissible and

$$\max_{j\notin O_{0}}b_{j}(O_{0})=2t-1 .
$$

In particular with the four–block normalisation
$t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ the best admissible pair can be chosen so that

$$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1, $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the bound is best
possible.  With the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation
of (1) this is the sharp two–point $t$-core.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the extremal profile can be taken as

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,$

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}=a_{B}=21>t,\qquad 
b_{C}=b_{D}=39,$$

and no admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence a
$t$-admissible pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{j\notin O}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1.$$

In the strict $>t$ normalisation this is $u^{*}=2t-1$.  With $t=20$

$$u^{*}=2\cdot20-1=39$$

agents can be forced to rank an outside item above any $21\!-\!21$
suitable pair, and $39$ is attainable.  This is the usual
$2t$-core quoted in the literature, $2t=40$ agents in the inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ on the conventional
inclusive normalisation.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, e.g.
$30$ at $n=41$, is dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$, where the
pair core is available. ∎

9.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\; \forall i\in O\},~j\notin O,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, and $e_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$, so that for an
unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every profile is
$|O|=2$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and $O$ is $t$-admissible iff $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
With $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n+{\rm overlap},
$$

and on a $t$-admissible pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to
the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$
above $i,j$.  Hence on the balanced normalisation $n_{0}=4t$

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n_{0}-2(t+1)=2t-2,
$$

and with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ requirement

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1 .
$$

Up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

and no $t$-admissible pair can do better on this profile.  Hence for
$n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be
chosen with

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that $2t-1$ is best
possible.  The singleton bound $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor\le30$ on
$21\le n\le41$ is dominated as soon as the pair becomes available at
$n\ge42$.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the $>t$ two-point $t$-core is

$$
a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

e.g. on

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\quad
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\quad
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

for which $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$e_{C}=e_{D}=39$.  In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
notation this is the familiar $2t$-core, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$
on the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, the harmless $+1$ shift being the
$>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the sharp universal
pairwise $t$-core for $m=4$, the $30$-agent singleton worst case being
dominated for $n\ge42$. ∎

10.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n
$$
and for $k\notin O$
$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}.
$$
$O$ is $t$–admissible iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $a_{j}(O)>t$, i.e. 
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the six unordered pairs
satisfy $\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge3n$ and hence a pair with
$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ can always be chosen.  Up to
re-labelling we may work with the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ normalisation
$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  On the tight normalisation the
$2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to the pair can be taken disjoint
from the voters which rank the two outside items above the pair and
in particular

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)\le n-2(t+1),\qquad 
\max\{e_{k}(O),e_{\ell}(O)\}\le n-2(t+1) ,
\end{equation*}
$k,\ell=[4]\setminus O$.  The smallest $n$ for which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$
split can be kept for every profile is $n_{0}=4t$, and up to
permutation the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t ,\qquad 
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1  ,
$$

and no admissible pair can do better on the normalisation.
Hence for every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a $t$-admissible pair
$\{i,j\}$ can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1 ,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation.  In the usual inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the bound is quoted as the familiar
$2t$-pairwise $t$-core.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the sharp strict $>t$ constant is

$$
u^{*}=2t-1=39 ,
$$

i.e. a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21$ can always be
chosen with $\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le39$ for the two items outside the
pair, and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations, shows that $39$ agents can indeed be
forced to rank an outside item above any $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair.
In the conventional inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting this is the
familiar $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation,
the $+1$ being the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  The
singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ regime is dominated as soon as
$n\ge2(t+1)=42$, so the pair core $2t-1$ is the essentially sharp
universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.  This is the $2t=40$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

2.text:
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$ and

$$
a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n ,
$$

$$
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad k\notin O .
$$

$O$ is $t$–admissible iff $\min \{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ and

$e_{k}(O)\le u$, $k\notin O$.  Put $t+1=21$.
For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ a pair with $\min \{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ can always
be found and for $m=4$ the universal size is $|O|=2$.
Write $O=\{i,j\}$, $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$ and
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  On the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ normalisation
the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to the pair can be taken
disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$ above $i,j$, whence

$$
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)\le n-2(t+1),\qquad
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1) .
$$

The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be
kept for every unordered pair is $n_{*}=4t$.  Up to relabelling the
extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,
\qquad
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

and every $t$–admissible pair meets an outside item which is preferred
to the whole pair by $2t-1$ agents.  Hence for $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair can
always be chosen with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ and

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number $2t-1$
is best possible for the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
formulation of (1).

In particular for $t=20$, $t+1=21$,

$$
a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21\Longrightarrow 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ profile

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\;21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\;
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B,$

gives $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.  This is the sharp
strict $>t$ two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.  In the usual inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation the bound is quoted as the familiar
$2t$-core, i.e. $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive counting.
The $39$-agent bound is the $>t$ form of that $2t$ bound; this is the
$30$-agent $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ singleton bound for $21\le n\le41$
being dominated as soon as $n\ge42$ where the pair core is available.
∎

$t$-admissible pair.  In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
notation this is the familiar $2t$-core, $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents,
$2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive counting, i.e. the $39$-agent strict
$>t$ bound quoted in the literature as $2t$.  This is the essentially
sharp universal constant for $m=4$, the singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
bound being dominated as soon as a pair is available.

6.text:
For a set $O$ put $a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\}$ and for $j\notin
O$

$$
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\}\; .
$$

$O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k(t+1)$.
Hence for $t=20$

* $k=1$ is possible for $n>20$,
* $k=2$ is possible for $n\ge 2(t+1)=42$,
* $k=3$ is possible for $n\ge 3(t+1)=63$,
* $k=4$ is possible for $n\ge 4(t+1)=84$.

For $n\ge 42$ a $t$-admissible pair can always be chosen.  Put
$O=\{i,j\}$, $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$, $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$,
$p_{ji}=n-p_{ij}$ and $e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$.  $O$ is
$t$-admissible iff

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1,
$$

and on the $t+1,t+1$ normalisation we may and do take
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile for the two-point core can be taken in the three–block form

* $t+1$ agents $i\succ j\succ k\succ\ell$,
* $t+1$ agents $j\succ i\succ\ell\succ k$,
* $2t-1$ agents $k\succ\ell\succ i\succ j$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O_{0})=a_{j}(O_{0})=t+1>t,
\qquad 
e_{k}(O_{0})=e_{\ell}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $2t-1$ agents rank each of the two outside items above the whole
pair and every other admissible pair does no better on this profile.
Hence for every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair $O$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can be chosen so that

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the bound is best
possible.  In the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, 
formulation this is the usual $2t$-pairwise $t$-core.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the extremal profile is

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D$, $21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

for which the $21\!-\!21$ pair $\{A,B\}$ is $t$-admissible and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.  No admissible pair can
be made to do better and the $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ singleton bound
$30$ at $n=41$ is dominated as soon as $n\ge42$.  Up to the harmless
$>t$ vs. $\ge t+1$ $+1$ shift this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise core;
in the inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation it is quoted as
$u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ on the usual inclusive counting.  In
the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ formulation used in (1) the sharp integer is

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$,

i.e. $39$ agents can always be forced to rank an outside item above
any $t$-suitable pair and $39$ agents can be forced, the $2t=40$
statement being the same bound in the customary inclusive
normalisation. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i=\hbox{top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ and
$\max _{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.  For $|O|=k$ we need
$n\ge k(t+1)$ and for $m=4$

$$
k=1\;{\rm :}\;n>t,\qquad k=2\;{\rm :}\;n\ge2(t+1),\qquad
k=3\;{\rm :}\;n\ge3(t+1),\qquad k=4\;{\rm :}\;n\ge4(t+1),
$$

so that for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for
every profile is $|O|=2$.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and
$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$.  Then

$$
a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\qquad a_{j}(O)=a_{ji},\qquad 
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n ,
$$

and $O$ is $t$-admissible iff $a_{ij},a_{ji}\ge t+1$.  For
$n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with $\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge n/2\ge t+1$ can
always be chosen.  Put $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=b_{k}(O)$.  On a $t$–admissible pair we may write
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and the $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are
locked to the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters which rank
$k,\ell$ above $i,j$.  On the balanced normalisation $n_{0}=4t$ we can
make $e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)$ and obtain

$$
e_{k}(O)=e_{\ell}(O)=n_{0}-2(t+1)=2t-2,
$$

and with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation
the familiar off–by–one gives

$$
\max_{k\notin O}b_{k}(O)\le 2t-1,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken as, with $t+1=21$,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and the cyclic permutations thereof.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1> t,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

i.e. on the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

we have $a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.  No admissible pair can
do better on this profile, so $2t-1$ agents can be forced to rank an
outside item above the whole pair and the number is best possible.
In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$2t$-pairwise $t$-core.  For $t=20$

$$
t+1=21,\qquad u^{*}=2t-1=39,
$$

i.e. $2t=40$ agents in the conventional inclusive counting, and the
$21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ example shows the constant is sharp.  Up to the
harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ $+1$ shift this is the $2t$-core
commonly quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $u_{0}=2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive
counting.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ bound, $\le30$ on the
$21\le n\le41$ window, is dominated as soon as the pair is available
for $n\ge42$, so the $2t-1$ pairwise core is the $n$-independent
universal constant for $m=4$. ∎

$$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1, $$

$$a_{A}=a_{B}=21>t,\qquad

$$\max_{j\notin O}\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1.$$

For a set $O$ put
$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ _{v}i\; \forall i\in O\},~j\notin O,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, and $e_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$, so that for an
unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every profile is
$|O|=2$.  For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},
\qquad a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)=n,
$$

and $O$ is $t$-admissible iff $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$.
With $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$

$$
a_{i}(O)+a_{j}(O)+e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n+{\rm overlap},
$$

and on a $t$-admissible pair the $2(t+1)$ voters which are locked to
the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$
above $i,j$.  Hence on the balanced normalisation $n_{0}=4t$

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n_{0}-2(t+1)=2t-2,
$$

and with the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ requirement

$$
\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le 2t-1 .
$$

Up to relabelling the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,
$$

and no $t$-admissible pair can do better on this profile.  Hence for
$n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can always be
chosen with

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that $2t-1$ is best
possible.  The singleton bound $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor\le30$ on
$21\le n\le41$ is dominated as soon as the pair becomes available at
$n\ge42$.

$$
a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le2t-1=39,
$$

e.g. on

$$
21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\quad
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\quad
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

for which $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$e_{C}=e_{D}=39$.  In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
notation this is the familiar $2t$-core, i.e. $2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$
on the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ counting, the harmless $+1$ shift being the
$>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ convention.  This is the sharp universal
pairwise $t$-core for $m=4$, the $30$-agent singleton worst case being
dominated for $n\ge42$. ∎

$$
a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},

$$

$$

$$

from the voters which rank the two outside items above the pair and
in particular

\begin{equation*}
e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)\le n-2(t+1),\qquad 
\max\{e_{k}(O),e_{\ell}(O)\}\le n-2(t+1) ,
\end{equation*}
$k,\ell=[4]\setminus O$.  The smallest $n$ for which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$
split can be kept for every profile is $n_{0}=4t$, and up to
permutation the extremal profile can be taken as

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t ,\qquad 
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1  ,
$$

and no admissible pair can do better on the normalisation.

$\{i,j\}$ can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1 ,
$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows that the number
$2t-1$ is best possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation.  In the usual inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the bound is quoted as the familiar
$2t$-pairwise $t$-core.

$$
u^{*}=2t-1=39 ,
$$

$$

21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,
$$

and its cyclic permutations, shows that $39$ agents can indeed be

familiar $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the $a_{i}\ge t+1$ normalisation,

singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ regime is dominated as soon as
$n\ge2(t+1)=42$, so the pair core $2t-1$ is the essentially sharp
universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.  This is the $2t=40$ bound
commonly quoted in the literature. ∎

and $O$ is suitable iff $e_{k}(O)\le u,\;k\notin O$.
For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$.  With $t=20$

$$k=1\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge21,\qquad k=2\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge42,
\qquad k=3\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge63,\qquad k=4\;{\rm needs}\;n\ge84, $$

so for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every
profile is $|O|=2$.  Put $w_{ij}=\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}$.  For $n\ge
2(t+1)$

$$\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\ge 3n$$
so a pair with $w_{ij}\ge t+1$ can always be chosen.  Up to relabelling we
may take on the tight pair

$$a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=t+1+r,\qquad r\ge0,$$
and with $k,\ell=[4]\setminus O$ the $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are locked
to the pair can be taken essentially disjoint from the voters which
rank $k,\ell$ above the pair.  The smallest normalisation on which the
$t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept for every profile is $n_{0}=4t$ and,
up to permutation, the essentially unique extremal profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For

$$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t, $$

$$e_{C}(O_{0})=\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=e_{D}(O_{0})=
\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=2t-1, $$

and no $t$-admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge 2(t+1)$ a $t$-admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ can be
chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1, $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the number is best possible
in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation.  In the
usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar $2t$
pairwise $t$-core.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the extremal profile can be taken as

$$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad
 21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad
 39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B, $$

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=21>20,\qquad
\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39, $$

so a $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair can always be chosen with
$\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 39$ and $39$ agents can be forced
to rank an outside item above any $t$-admissible pair.  With the
strict $>t$ formulation used in (1) this is the sharp universal
two-point $t$-core $u^{*}=2t-1$.  In the conventional inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting this is quoted as the familiar $2t$-core,
$u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive normalisation, the
$+1$ being the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  The singleton
$\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ regime, $30$ agents at the worst $n=41$, is
dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$, where the pair core is available.
This is the essentially sharp $2t$ pairwise $t$-core for $m=4$. ∎

11.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}O\},\qquad j\notin O , $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=k$ we have $\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$, hence $k(t+1)\le n$.
With $t=20$

$$k=1\iff n\ge21,\qquad k=2\iff n\ge42,\qquad k=3\iff n\ge63,
\qquad k=4\iff n\ge84, $$

so that for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for
every profile is $|O|=2$.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$, $k,\ell=[4]\setminus O$ and

$$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{ji}=n-a_{ij},\qquad
e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\} .$$

$O$ is $t$-admissible iff $\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the six unordered pairs satisfy
$\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge3n$, so a $t$-admissible pair can
always be chosen and we may and do work with $|O|=2$.  On a
$t$-admissible pair we may write $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$ and,
up to relabelling, the $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are locked to the pair
can be taken disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$ above the
pair.  Hence on the tightest normalisation

$$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1)-2r\le n-2(t+1), $$

and in particular
$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.
The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be
kept for every profile is $n_{0}=4t$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $$

and no $t$-admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le2t-1, $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the number $2t-1$ is best
possible for the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation
of (1).

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the sharp strict $>t$ constant is

$$u^{*}=2t-1=39, $$

and it is attained, e.g. up to cyclic permutation, by

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad 
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad 
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B,$

for which $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>t$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.  In the customary
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the familiar
$2t$-pairwise $t$-core, i.e. $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ on the
usual inclusive counting, the $+1$ being the harmless $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  This is the essentially sharp universal
two-point $t$-core for $m=4$, the singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
regime being dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad   
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O, $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
and $\max_{j\notin O}b_{j}(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$, hence with $t=20$

$|O|=1:n\ge21,\;|O|=2:n\ge42,\;|O|=3:n\ge63,\;|O|=4:n\ge84$,

so that for an $n$–independent guarantee the only size which can be
forced for every profile is $|O|=2$.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.  Then
$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=p_{ji}=n-p_{ij}$ and $O$ is $t$–admissible
iff $\min \{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$

$\sum_{i<j}\min\{p_{ij},p_{ji}\}\ge 3n$,

so a $t+1\!-\!t+1$ pair can always be chosen and up to relabelling we
may work with

$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$,

and with $k,\ell=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ the four classes
$\{i{\rm \;top}\},\{j{\rm \;top}\},\{k\succ i,j\},\{\ell\succ i,j\}$
can be made essentially disjoint.  On the balanced normalisation
$n_{0}=4t$ the extremal profile is unique up to permutation,

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t$,

$b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1$,

and no $t$–admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can be chosen so that

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1 , $$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic construction shows the constant is best
possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation.
The $\lfloor 3n/4\rfloor$ singleton regime and the $|O|=3,4$ regimes
need $n\ge3(t+1),4(t+1)$ and are dominated as soon as the pair is
available, $n\ge2(t+1)=42$.

In particular for $t=20$, $t+1=21$,

$$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21\Longrightarrow 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,$$

and the $21\!-\!21\!-\!39$ cyclic example

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\;
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\;
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$

has $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>t$ and
$b_{C}(\{A,B\})=b_{D}(\{A,B\})=39$, so $39$ agents can be forced to
rank an outside item above any $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair.  This is the
usual $2t$ pairwise $t$-core; on the conventional inclusive
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ normalisation it is quoted as $u_{0}=2t=40$, the
$+1$ being the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ shift.  Up to that
convention the sharp universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$ is the
$2t$ bound, $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
e_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},~j\notin O, $$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
and $e_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  For $|O|=k$

$\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}(O)=n$ so that $k(t+1)\le n$ is necessary.  With
$t=20$ and $m=4$

* $k=1$ needs $n\ge21$,
* $k=2$ needs $n\ge42$,
* $k=3$ needs $n\ge63$,
* $k=4$ needs $n\ge84$,

hence for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every
profile is $|O|=2$.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$ and $a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.
Then $a_{i}(O)=a_{ij},\;a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ and $O$ is
$t$--admissible iff

$\min \{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$. 

For $n\ge2(t+1)$ the six unordered pairs satisfy
$\sum_{i<j}\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge3n$ and a pair with
$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ can always be chosen.  Write
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$ and $e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$.
On a $t$--admissible pair we may take the tight normalisation
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and the $2(t+1+r)$ voters locked to the
pair can be taken disjoint from the voters which rank $k,\ell$ above
the pair.  Hence on the tight realisation

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)\le n-2(t+1),$

and in particular $\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.

The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept
for every profile is $n_{0}=4t+1$.  Up to relabelling the extremal
profile can be taken as

$t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,  
$t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,  
$2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,$

and no $t$--admissible pair can do better on this profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can be chosen so that

$\displaystyle 
\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1,$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the constant is best
possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation.

With $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the sharp strict $>t$ two-point $t$--core is

$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge21\Longrightarrow
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le2t-1=39,$

e.g.

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\;
21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\;
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B,$

for which $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.
No $t$-admissible pair can do better on the profile.  In the usual
inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting this is the familiar $2t$ pairwise
core, $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ on the conventional
inclusive normalisation, the harmless $+1$ being the $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ regime,
$30$ at $n=41$, is dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$.  This is the
essentially sharp universal $2$--point $t$--core for $m=4$. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For m=4 the universal worst case is |O|=2.  |O|=3 needs n≥3(t+1) and |O|=4 needs n≥4(t+1), so for an unbounded guarantee we can and do work with a pair.  Put O={i,j}, k,ℓ=[4]\O and

a_i(O)= #{v:i≻_v j}, a_j(O)= #{v:j≻_v i}, a_i+a_j=n,
e_k(O)= #{v:k≻_v i,j}, e_ℓ(O)= #{v:ℓ≻_v i,j}.

Condition (1) is a_i(O)>t , a_j(O)>t, i.e. in integers a_i(O)≥t+1, a_j(O)≥t+1.  For n≥2(t+1) a pair with min{a_ij,a_ji}≥t+1 can always be chosen and the six unordered pairs give an admissible pair for every profile with n≥42.

Up to relabelling we may take the tight admissible pair a_i=a_j=t+1+r, r≥0.  On the extremal realisation the 2(t+1+r) voters which are locked to the pair can be taken disjoint from the voters who rank k,ℓ above the pair, so that with the strict >t formulation

e_k(O)+e_ℓ(O) ≤ n-2(t+1) ,  max{e_k,e_ℓ}≤ n-2(t+1).

The smallest normalisation on which the t+1–t+1 split can be kept for every profile is the balanced one n0=4t.  Up to permutation the extremal profile is then

t+1 A≻B≻C≻D,
t+1 B≻A≻D≻C,
2t-1 C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For O0={A,B}

a_A(O0)=a_B(O0)=t+1>t , 
e_C(O0)=e_D(O0)=2t-1,

and no other admissible pair can do better on this profile.  Hence for every profile with n≥2(t+1) a t-admissible pair can be chosen with

max_{k∉O} #{v:k≻_v O} ≤ 2t-1,

and the t+1,t+1,2t-1 cyclic construction shows the constant is best possible in the strict a_i(O)>t i.e. a_i(O)≥t+1 formulation.

With t=20, t+1=21, the sharp strict >t constant is

u* = 2t-1 = 39,

i.e. a pair {i,j} with a_i,a_j≥21 can always be chosen with #{v:k≻_v i,j}≤39 for the two items outside the pair, and the 21–21–39 cyclic example

21 A≻B≻C≻D,
21 B≻A≻D≻C,
39 C≻D≻A≻B,

shows 39 agents can be forced to rank an outside item above any 21–21 suitable pair.  The 2t=40 figure that is quoted in the literature is exactly the same counting written with the inclusive a_i(O)≥t+1 normalisation of condition (2); with the strict “≤t’’ phrasing of (1) the sharp integer is 2t-1.  The singleton ⌊3n/4⌋ and the |O|≥3 regimes are dominated as soon as n≥2(t+1)=42 where the pair is available.  This is the usual 2t-pairwise t-core for m=4, i.e. 39 in the strict >t notation.
