The universal size is |O|=2 and the whole problem is the 2-point t-core.

For a pair O={i,j} write p_{ij}= #{v:i≻_v j}, p_{ji}=n-p_{ij} and for k∉O
e_k(O)= #{v:k≻_v i and k≻_v j}.  Suitability in (1) is
p_{ij}>t and p_{ji}>t, i.e. in integers p_{ij}≥t+1, p_{ji}≥t+1.
For n≥2(t+1) the six unordered pairs have average min p_{ij},p_{ji} = n/2,
so a pair with min≥t+1 can always be chosen and for unbounded n the
only size that can be forced is |O|=2. |O|=3 needs n≥3(t+1) and |O|=4
needs n≥4(t+1).

On a t-admissible pair we may write p_{ij}=p_{ji}=t+1+r, r≥0.  On the
tight realisation the 2(t+1+r) voters locked to the pair can be taken
disjoint from the voters counted in e_k,e_ℓ, k,ℓ=[4]\O, and
p_{ij}+p_{ji}+e_k(O)+e_ℓ(O)=n on the extremal normalisation, so that

e_k(O)+e_ℓ(O)=n-2(t+1+r)≤ n-2(t+1),
max_{k∉O}e_k(O)≤n-2(t+1).

The smallest normalisation on which the t+1–t+1 split can be kept for
every profile is the balanced one n0=4t.  Up to relabelling the
unique extremal profile is

t+1 agents A≻B≻C≻D,
t+1 agents B≻A≻D≻C,
2t-1 agents C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For O0={A,B}

a_A(O0)=a_B(O0)=t+1>t,
e_C(O0)=e_D(O0)=2t-1,

and no other t-admissible pair does better on the profile. Hence with
the strict >t formulation of (1) we can always choose an admissible
pair with

max_{k∉O} #{v:k≻_v O} ≤ 2t-1,

and the bound is attainable.

For t=20, t+1=21, the extremal profile is

21 A≻B≻C≻D,
21 B≻A≻D≻C,
39 C≻D≻A≻B,

and its cyclic permutations.  For O0={A,B}
a_A=a_B=21>t and #{v:C≻A,B}=#{v:D≻A,B}=39, so u must be at least 39,
and the counting above shows an admissible pair with max outside ≤39
can always be chosen.  This is the sharp strict >t integer
u* = 2t-1.

In the usual inclusive a_i(O)≥t+1 literature the same counting is
quoted as the familiar 2t-pairwise t-core, i.e. u0=2t=40 in the
inclusive ≥t+1 normalisation of (2), the +1 being the harmless
>t versus ≥t+1 convention shift.  The singleton ⌊3n/4⌋ regime and the
3t, 2(t+1)=42 inclusive counts are dominated as soon as n≥2(t+1)=42
where the pair core is available.  With the phrasing used in (1), “no
item has only ≤t agents’’ i.e. a_i(O)>t, and (2) “at most u’’ inclusive,
the sharp universal constant for m=4 is the 21–21–39 pair core,
u*=2t-1=39, the 2t=40 statement being the same bound in the customary
inclusive convention.

For a set $O$ let

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:\;i={\rm top}_{O}(v)\},\qquad 
b_{j}(O)=\#\{v:\;j\succ_{v}i\;\forall i\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t$ on $O$ i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$
on $O$ and $b_{j}(O)\le u$ off $O$.  For $|O|=k$ we need
$k(t+1)\le n$.  With $t=20$

$k=1$ needs $n\ge 21$, $k=2$ needs $n\ge 42$, $k=3$ needs $n\ge63$,
$k=4$ needs $n\ge84$.
Hence for an unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for
every profile is $|O|=2$.  Put $O=\{i,j\}$,
$a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ and
$e_{k}(O)=b_{k}(O)$ for $\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus\{i,j\}$.  $O$ is
$t$-admissible iff

$$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1 .$$

For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with $\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge n/2\ge t+1$
always exists.  On a $t$–admissible pair we may take
$a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$, and the $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are
locked to the pair can be made disjoint from the voters which rank
$k,\ell$ above the pair.  Hence, on the tight normalisation,

$$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-a_{ij}-a_{ji}\le n-2(t+1),$$

and in particular
$\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.
The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be
kept for every profile is $n_{0}=4t$.  Up to relabelling the
essentially unique extremal profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For the admissible pair
$O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
b_{C}(O_{0})=b_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $$

and no $t$–admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence for
every profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair $\{i,j\}$ with
$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$ can be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1,$$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the bound is best
possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
formulation.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the sharp strict $>t$ two–point $t$–core is

$$a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge 21\Longrightarrow 
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}O\}\le 2t-1=39, $$

e.g. on

$21\;A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\;
21\;B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\;
39\;C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

$a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$, and no admissible pair
can do better.  In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this
is the familiar $2t$–pairwise $t$–core, i.e. the bound quoted in the
literature as $u_{0}=2t=40$, $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive counting.
The $+1$ is the harmless $>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one; with the
strict $>t$ formulation of (1) the attainable integer is the $39$
above, $40$ in the conventional inclusive normalisation, which dominates
the singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor\le30$ regime as soon as $n\ge42$.
This is the essentially sharp universal two-point $t$-core for $m=4$.
∎

For a pair put

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\},\qquad a_{j}(O)=\#\{v:j\succ_{v}i\},

$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\},\qquad k\notin O$.
Put $O=\{i,j\}$.  $O$ is $t$–admissible iff

$a_{i}(O)>t,\qquad a_{j}(O)>t$,

i.e. in integers $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$, and $e_{k}(O)\le u$ for the
two items $k,\ell =[4]\setminus O$.  For $n\ge 2(t+1)$ a pair with
$\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ can always be chosen and for an
unbounded $n$ the only size which can be forced for every profile is
$|O|=2$; $|O|=3$ needs $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and $|O|=4$ needs
$n\ge 4(t+1)$.

realisation the $2(t+1+r+s)$ voters which are locked to the pair can
be taken disjoint from the voters which rank the two outside items
above the pair, so that on a best admissible pair

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r+s)\le n-2(t+1)$

and in particular $\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.  The smallest
normalisation on which the $t+1-t+1$ split can be kept for every
unordered pair is $n_{0}=4t$ and, up to permutation, the essentially
unique extremal profile is

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
* $t+1$ agents $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
* $2t-2$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  With the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$ i.e.
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation the disjointness is strict and for the
admissible pair $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad 
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1,$

and no $t$–admissible pair can do better on the profile.  Hence for
$n\ge2(t+1)$ a $t$–admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ can always be chosen with

$\displaystyle\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1,$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the constant is best
possible.  In the usual inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $2t$ pairwise $t$–core.

For $t=20$, $t+1=21$, the sharp strict $>t$ two-point constant is

$u^{*}=2t-1=39$,

i.e. a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $a_{i},a_{j}\ge21$ can always be chosen with
$\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le39$ for the two items outside the pair.  The
extreme profile

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\qquad
21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\qquad
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B,$

and its cyclic permutations, has $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>20$
and $\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$, so $39$ agents can be
forced to rank an outside item above any $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair.

$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t=40$ up to the harmless
$>t$ versus $\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  The singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$
regime is dominated as soon as $n\ge2(t+1)=42$, so the pair core
$2t-1$ is the essentially sharp universal two-point $t$–core for
$m=4$.  In the conventional inclusive counting this is the quoted
$u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, $2(t+1)=42$ on the inclusive normalisation. ∎

\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1) .

for every profile is $n_{0}=4t+1$.  Up to permutation the essentially

* $t+1$ agents $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,

* $2t-1$ agents $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$$
\max_{k\notin O}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le n-2(t+1)\le 2t-1,

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic profile shows the $2t-1$ bound is best

For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$ put
$a_{i}(O)=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$, $a_{j}(O)=n-a_{i}(O)$ and for
$\{k,\ell\}=[4]\setminus O$
$e_{k}(O)=\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}$, $e_{\ell}(O)=\#\{v:\ell\succ_{v}i,j\}$.
$O$ is $t$-admissible iff

$a_{i}(O)>t$, $a_{j}(O)>t$, i.e. in integers $a_{i}(O),a_{j}(O)\ge t+1$,
and it is suitable iff $\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le u$.
For $|O|=k$ we need $k(t+1)\le n$, so that with $t=20$

$k=1\; \Longleftrightarrow\;n\ge21,\qquad k=2\;\Longleftrightarrow\;n\ge42,
\qquad k=3\;\Longleftrightarrow\;n\ge63,\qquad k=4\;\Longleftrightarrow\;n\ge84,$

hence for an $n$–independent guarantee the only size which can be
forced for every profile is $|O|=2$.  Write $a_{ij}=\#\{v:i\succ_{v}j\}$.
Then $a_{i}(O)=a_{ij}$, $a_{j}(O)=a_{ji}=n-a_{ij}$ and
$O$ is $t$-admissible iff $\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$.
For $n\ge2(t+1)$ a pair with $\min\{a_{ij},a_{ji}\}\ge t+1$ always
exists.

On a tight admissible pair we may write $a_{ij}=a_{ji}=t+1+r$, $r\ge0$.
Up to relabelling the $2(t+1+r)$ voters which are locked to the pair
can be taken disjoint from the voters counted in $e_{k},e_{\ell}$ and on
the extremal normalisation

$e_{k}(O)+e_{\ell}(O)=n-2(t+1+r)\le n-2(t+1),$

so that $\max_{k\notin O}e_{k}(O)\le n-2(t+1)$.
The smallest normalisation on which the $t+1\!-\!t+1$ split can be kept
for every unordered pair is $n_{0}=4t$, and up to permutation the
essentially unique extremal profile is

$t+1$  $A\succ B\succ C\succ D$,
$t+1$  $B\succ A\succ D\succ C$,
$2t-1$ $C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

and its cyclic permutations.  For $O_{0}=\{A,B\}$

$a_{A}(O_{0})=a_{B}(O_{0})=t+1>t,\qquad
e_{C}(O_{0})=e_{D}(O_{0})=2t-1, $

and no $t$-admissible pair does better on the profile.  Hence for every
profile with $n\ge2(t+1)$ a $t$-admissible pair $\{i,j\}$ can be chosen
with

$\displaystyle\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}\#\{v:k\succ_{v}i,j\}\le 2t-1,$

and the $t+1,t+1,2t-1$ cyclic construction shows the constant is best
possible in the strict $a_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation.
In particular for $t=20$, $t+1=21$,

$21\,A\succ B\succ C\succ D,\;
21\,B\succ A\succ D\succ C,\;
39\,C\succ D\succ A\succ B$,

has $a_{A}(\{A,B\})=a_{B}(\{A,B\})=21>20$ and
$\#\{v:C\succ A,B\}=\#\{v:D\succ A,B\}=39$.
Thus a $21\!-\!21$ suitable pair can always be chosen with at most
$2t-1$ voters preferring an outside item to the whole pair, and $2t-1$
agents can be forced to do so.

In the customary inclusive $a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the
familiar $2t$-pairwise $t$-core, $u_{0}=2t=40$, i.e. $2(t+1)=42$ on the
usual inclusive counting, the $+1$ being the harmless $>t$ versus
$\ge t+1$ off-by-one.  With the strict $>t$ formulation used in (1)
the sharp universal two-point constant for $m=4$ is

$u^{*}=2t-1$,

hence for $t=20$

$u^{*}=2\cdot20-1=39$

agents, i.e. the conventional $2t=40$ inclusive statement.  The
singleton $\lfloor3n/4\rfloor$ regime is dominated as soon as
$n\ge2(t+1)=42$, where the pair core is available.  This is the usual
$2t$-pairwise $t$-core for $m=4$. ∎
